sens: Action of crushing, trampling with force
Brutal domination, oppression of a powerful people
Situation of turmoil and destruction
State of one who is defeated, annihilated
H4001.detail:
1. The word describes the concrete action of crushing, of trampling something or someone under its weight: it is the brutal trampling that crushes everything in its path. Isaiah 18:2 and 18:7 speak of a nation "that crushes everything," an image of a power that destroys mercilessly all it encounters.
2. In a figurative sense, it is the overwhelming domination of a strong people over others, oppression by brute force. This formidable nation imposes its will through terror and destruction.
3. The word also designates the turmoil, destruction, and chaos that result. In Isaiah 22:5, the "crushing" accompanies cries of distress and the demolition of walls: it is the collapse of all order.
4. More broadly, it is the state of one who is defeated, broken, annihilated by a superior force — the complete ruin of resistance.
H4001.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root בוס (bous), which means "to trample, to crush." This root evokes the physical image of a foot that crushes. The form משבוסה (mevu-sah) is a derived noun that names the action or state resulting from this brutal trampling. The same root appears in other biblical contexts to describe acts of violent domination.
H4001.emploi: The word appears three times in Isaiah, always to describe overwhelming power. In verses 18:2 and 18:7, it qualifies a formidable nation whose strength lies in its ability to dominate and destroy. In verse 22:5, it is a judgment from God: the crushing is no longer a human power, but the destruction that God sends — turmoil, confusion, and ruin of Jerusalem's defenses. The word always expresses the idea of an irresistible force that crushes, devastates, oppresses.
H4001.portee: This word reminds the believer that human power, no matter how impressive, is fragile before God. It also teaches that the brutal oppression of peoples provokes divine judgment. For those who suffer from the crushing, the text announces that only God can stop this violence and restore justice.

sens: point where water springs from a source
place where one can drink and quench thirst
place of life and fertility in the desert
gift of God that preserves life
H4002.detail:
1. A source is the natural point from which water springs from the earth. In Ecclesiastes 12, the word literally describes the "source" to which the bucket breaks: it is the place where one draws water that allows for daily life.
2. It is a place where one can drink and quench thirst, far from fatigue and death. Isaiah 49 shows this: those who have water sources do not hunger or thirst, despite the desert and the sun that torment them.
3. The source represents life and fertility in the midst of the arid desert. In Isaiah 35, the dry land transforms into water sources: the image is that of the barren land becoming habitable and generous, where reeds and rushes grow where jackals once lived.
4. It is a gift from God that preserves His children. When God leads to water sources, He shows Himself as compassionate and the provider of life itself.
H4002.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that means "to spring forth" or "to come out." It is a noun that specifically designates the point of emergence of water, where it naturally appears from the ground. The same word is used for anything that springs or wells up from the earth.
H4002.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the literal sense of a water source. In the two passages from Isaiah (35:7 and 49:10), the context is that of a promise of salvation: God transforms the arid desert into a fertile garden for His people. In Ecclesiastes 12:8, the word enters into a poetic description of the aging of man. The word always marks a life issue: absence of source = death and desert; presence of source = life, fertility, hope.
H4002.portee: The water source in Scripture symbolizes God's vital gift to His people. It reminds us that without God, humanity is lost in the desert; with Him, even sterility transforms into abundance. It is a word that invites trust: he who places himself under God's guidance will lack neither bread nor water.

sens: That which is stripped bare, emptied of its contents
Action of pillaging, completely ravaging
State of desolation and ruin that results
Destruction that inspires terror and annihilation
H4003.detail: 1. The word literally designates that which is emptied, that which has lost what it contained — a city from which all goods have been taken, a place left empty. In Nahum 2:11, the prophet cries: "They pillage, they devastate, they ravage!" — it is the action of taking everything away, leaving nothing behind. 2. It is the act of massive destruction that accompanies war and conquest: not only killing, but stripping bare, leaving empty. The context of Nahum shows inhabitants whose "hearts are crushed, knees tremble" in the face of this total ravaging. 3. The result is a profound desolation: the emptiness becomes visible, the nothingness where there was once wealth, order, life. The devastation is not a mere damage; it is an annihilation that marks the minds.
H4003.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root (בוק) that means "to be empty, to be devastated." The same family produces words for emptiness and vacuity. It is the image of hollowness, of nothingness — everything that was full and solid becomes hollow. The form used here is that of the action noun, expressing the act or state of devastation.
H4003.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nahum 2:11. The prophet Nahum announces the destruction of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, by the Medes and Babylonians. He depicts the rush of warriors entering the city: "They pillage, they devastate, they ravage!" The word here translates total chaos, the systematic action of emptying the city of its treasures and its inhabitants. It is a cry of distress and absolute destruction, a moment of collective annihilation.
H4003.portee: This word invites the reader to understand the force of God's judgment on evil: destruction is not partial or temporary; it is radical. Nineveh, a city of violence and pride, will be emptied, devastated, reduced to nothing. For the Christian, this reminds us that evil and injustice have an end, and that divine justice is real and powerful.

sens: What is best, most excellent in a whole
The most chosen, the most beautiful or the strongest elements
H4004.detail:
1. The word designates what is chosen as the best in a group: elite cities are the most important and fortified (2 Kings 3:19), the "beautiful" cedars are the most magnificent of Lebanon (2 Kings 19:23). It is excellence, superiority.
2. By extension, it characterizes anything that stands out from the lot by its quality: the best fields of a territory, the noblest trees of a region. The word expresses a hierarchy: among a thousand cities, some are "elite"; among a thousand cedars, some are "beautiful" — the foremost in their category.
H4004.origine: This word is a spelling variant of מִבְחָר (miv.char, H4005), which comes from the verb בָּחַר (ba.char) meaning "to choose." The starting idea is therefore that of what is chosen, what is selected because it is better than the rest. All words in the same family express this notion of selection and preferential quality.
H4004.emploi: This word appears twice in the Bible, only in 2 Kings. In 2 Kings 3:19, it applies to elite cities that will be destroyed during a military campaign — these are the most important strategic targets. In 2 Kings 19:23, it qualifies the most beautiful cedars and cypresses of Lebanon that the king of Nineveh claims he will cut down. In both cases, it is about targeting or boasting what is most excellent: the major fortifications on one side, the noblest trees on the other. The context is each time one of strength, conquest, and superiority.
H4004.portee: This word invites discernment of the hierarchy of values. In 2 Kings 3:19, the methodical destruction of elite cities reminds us that no place, however fortified, escapes God's judgment. In 2 Kings 19:23, the pretension of a king to cut down the most beautiful cedars symbolizes the pride of one who believes himself more powerful than the Creator Himself — a presumption that will be broken. The Christian sees that God alone decides what endures and what falls.

sens: What is most excellent, most beautiful in its kind
What is chosen among several because it is considered superior
The elite of a group, what it has that is most eminent
H4005.detail:
1. The best designates what is most excellent and most beautiful in a given category. When the Assyrian boasts of conquest, he speaks of cutting "the most beautiful of his cypress trees" (Isaiah 37:24): he means the most magnificent, the most imposing. Similarly, the trees of Eden that are "the most beautiful and the best of Lebanon" (Ezekiel 31:16) embody supreme excellence, the pinnacle of creation.
2. The best can also mean what is voluntarily selected for its superiority. God chooses a place for His name to dwell, and "the chosen offerings" (Deuteronomy 12:11) are presented to Him: these are the best offerings, selected because they are worthy of the Lord. Likewise, when one fills a pot with "the best bones" (Ezekiel 24:4), one takes the best parts of the animal.
3. The best also designates the elite of a people or an army, what is most precious and strongest. "The elite of his youth" of Moab "is slaughtered" (Jeremiah 48:15): these are the bravest young warriors, and their death is a disaster for the land.
H4005.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to choose, to select." The word mivchar thus originally designates what has been chosen, what is the result of a selection. This idea of choice naturally carries with it the notion of excellence: one always chooses what one considers to be the best. The concepts of "choosing" and "best" are thus inseparable in this word.
H4005.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and also in Exodus and Deuteronomy. It applies to various realities: the most beautiful trees (Isaiah 37:24 and Ezekiel 31:16), the best bones of the meat (Ezekiel 24:4), the most precious offerings presented to God (Deuteronomy 12:11), or the elite of a population, particularly the young warriors (Jeremiah 48:15). In all these cases, the word emphasizes distinction, excellence, and often the idea that what is best is what is most worthy, most noble, or most formidable. It is a word of a formal register that highlights superior quality.
H4005.portee: This word reminds us that God does not settle for the ordinary: He chooses the best for His worship and service. When we bring to the Lord "the chosen offerings" (Deuteronomy 12:11), we understand that our worship must be sincere and generous, that our first impulse must be to give the best, not the leftovers. At the same time, the fate of Moab's "elite" warns us that human greatness and carnal superiority last only a moment before divine judgment.

sens: Warrior in the service of King David
H4006.detail: Mibchar is one of the renowned warriors who served David. He appears in the official list of the "mighty men" of the king, alongside seasoned military leaders. His name means "the chosen one" in Hebrew, which fits well for an elite warrior: David only retained the best to form his guard and elite troops (1 Chronicles 11:38).
H4006.origine: The name Mibchar comes from the Hebrew root that means "to choose," "to prefer" — hence "the chosen one." It is a name that reflects the idea of selection and excellence, very appropriate for designating a top fighter at the court of a great warrior king.
H4006.emploi: Mibchar is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:38, where he is listed among David's mighty warriors. He is identified as the son of Hagri. His unique appearance, in this context of war and strength, shows his role as a military leader of secondary but recognized importance in the royal army.

sens: That in which one places their hope, the object of their expectation
State of assurance or security placed in someone or something
Expectation, what one hopes to obtain or anticipates from the future
H4007.detail:
1. The word concretely designates that in which someone places their hope or trust — the goal on which one counts to be saved or helped. To the Israelites who rely on Egypt, Isaiah reproaches them for having placed their trust in an ally who will disappoint them: "the object of our expectation, on which we had counted to be rescued" (Isaiah 20:6). It is a dependence, a support that one expects.
2. The word also expresses the state of assurance one feels when relying on someone. The Israelites "gloried in it" because they had an open trust in Egypt. It is a certainty one carries within: one walks with head held high because one believes in their protector (Isaiah 20:5).
3. It can also mean the hope or expectation itself — the hope one nurtures for the future. Ekron will see "its hope confounded" (Zechariah 9:5) when the expected help does not come. It is what one looks toward with certainty.
H4007.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to see, to look." The form mabbat literally means "that toward which one looks" or "that on which one sets their gaze" — that is, that in which one places their eyes and heart, what one watches for with assurance. The image evokes someone who turns and looks toward their awaited savior.
H4007.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in passages of judgment. Isaiah uses it twice to criticize those who place their trust in Egypt instead of trusting God: this false trust will not save them from judgment (Isaiah 20:5-6). Zechariah uses it once to announce that the coastal cities of Canaan will see their hope annihilated when the Messiah-King conquers the land (Zechariah 9:5). In all cases, it is a word of disappointment: trust placed in the wrong place collapses.
H4007.portee: This word invites the believer to examine where they truly place their trust. The prophets warn: counting on the powers of the world — wealth, human allies, political systems — is dangerous and vain. True trust must be in God alone, who never disappoints. The word also reminds us that everything in which we place our hope will one day be revealed: it will either be stable and salvific, or fragile and deceitful.

sens: Word spoken without thinking, which escapes from the mouth without control
Commitment or vow made hastily, without weighing the consequences
Promise or declaration that binds the one who uttered it, even if it was said lightly
H4008.detail:
1. The word refers to a word that escapes, that comes out of the mouth without having been weighed in advance — a spontaneous, uncontrolled word. The image is that of something that escapes, that flees, like water flowing between fingers. It is a thoughtless word, spoken in the heat of the moment (Numbers 30:7).
2. It often refers to a vow or commitment made hastily, without consideration of the consequences — a promise that one regrets afterward. The text in Numbers speaks of vows and verbal commitments that can be annulled by the husband or father depending on the circumstances.
3. Although it is lightly escaped, this word has legal force: it binds the one who pronounced it. This is why the Lord forgives the one whose husband annuls the commitment (Numbers 30:9) — forgiveness is necessary because the word, even hasty, had created an obligation.
H4008.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to escape" or "to split." It is formed to designate what escapes from the mouth — a word that departs without restraint. It is a term specific to the realm of hasty words and thoughtless vows in the legislation of the Pentateuch.
H4008.emploi: The word appears only twice in the entire Hebrew Bible, exclusively in chapter 30 of Leviticus (Numbers 30:7 and 30:9 according to the Segond). It is at the heart of the law concerning the vows of married women and young girls. The Law provides that if a woman pronounces a vow or verbal commitment — an escaped word — her husband can annul it on the day he becomes aware of it. This context shows that the term precisely designates spontaneous words and hasty commitments, which create an obligation before the Lord but can be questioned by the authority of the father or husband in cases provided by the Law.
H4008.portee: This word reminds us that every word counts — even one that escapes thoughtlessly creates a moral and spiritual obligation. It invites caution regarding vows and promises: "Beware of making thoughtless vows" could be its message. For the Christian reader, it emphasizes the importance of mastering one's tongue and weighing one's words, which the Epistle of James will powerfully reiterate.

sens: Act of confiding, of trusting someone or something
That in which one places their trust, what supports us
State of security and tranquility that results from it
Refuge, shelter where one finds safety
H4009.detail: 1. The act of entrusting one's fate to someone or something: it is the inner movement by which one surrenders to protection. In Proverbs 22:19, we are invited to place our trust in the Lord — it is the gesture of one who gives themselves up. 2. The object of this trust — what supports and carries us: in Job 31:24, gold becomes a false object of trust, a deceptive hope; in Proverbs 14:26, the fear of the Lord becomes a solid support for the one who fears God. 3. The inner state that results from it: a feeling of security and stability. Isaiah 32:18 depicts safe dwellings, a world inhabited by peace, where trust creates lasting tranquility. 4. Sometimes the refuge itself, the place of safety where one finds protection — a moral or spiritual fortress in the face of dangers.
H4009.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to be confident, to trust," with the idea of leaning on something or someone. It is related to the image of finding a point of support, a stable support. This root expresses the action of turning to a source of strength and stability, as one leans against a solid wall. Biblical trust never rests on emptiness: it always has an object.
H4009.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and the Book of Job. In the Wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs), it often designates false trust — that placed in wealth or works, which collapses like a spider's web (Job 8:14). But it can also describe just trust, founded on the fear of God and His promise. In Isaiah, this trust leads to tangible security: solid houses, real peace. Among the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel), it becomes the criterion of true worship — trusting in God rather than in idols or human alliances. The meaning oscillates between the source of trust (its object), the act of confiding, and the state of security that arises from it.
H4009.portee: This word teaches the believer that trust is the very heart of faith. It is not an abstract notion, but a concrete act: one must identify in whom or in what they place it. The Bible distinguishes between false trusts — wealth, men, idols — and the only solid trust, that which rests on God and His Word. Learning this word confronts us with the question: where is your true support?

sens: Action of relieving, of easing a pain or sorrow
That which soothes or comforts the afflicted heart
Joy or cheerfulness that brings comfort
H4010.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the action of relieving, of bringing respite to one who suffers. In Jeremiah 8:18, the prophet, overwhelmed with sorrow because of the misfortunes of his people, seeks something that could relieve his heart — which is why he says, "I wish to relieve my pain."
2. By extension, it refers to what comforts and soothes: a gentle word, a friendly presence, or simply a moment of rest when one is exhausted.
3. The word also evokes cheerfulness, joy, or the light of a smile that temporarily makes one forget sadness — it is a softening of grief through something lighter.
H4010.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of shining, radiating, or illuminating. This is why it carries within it the image of a light that chases away darkness, of a smile or cheerfulness that brightens a sad face. The same family of words can evoke clarity or brilliance, hence this sense of what comforts and restores brightness to the afflicted heart.
H4010.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 8:18. The prophet Jeremiah, seeing the spiritual and moral ruin of Judah, is overwhelmed with grief for his people. In the face of this inner distress, he expresses the desire for relief — something that could lighten his burden. The unique use of the word shows how precious relief is for one who endures suffering.
H4010.portee: This word reminds us that spiritual and moral pain is real and profound — it should not be denied or minimized. It also speaks to our legitimate need for comfort and relief when we are afflicted. At the same time, it invites us to seek what can truly uplift us: not a superficial distraction, but a true consolation that addresses the heart in its depth.

sens: Disposition and arrangement of the elements of a construction
Organization of the whole of a building or a city
General shape and plan of a built work
H4011.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the way in which stones, walls, and floors are arranged and assembled to form a building. It conveys the idea of physical composition and material organization. In Ezekiel 40:2, the prophet sees "like a city built" on the mountain: he contemplates its structure, its overall arrangement.

2. It extends to the overall plan of a construction: the way it is conceived, divided into parts, and hierarchized. The word emphasizes less the materials themselves than their logical and coherent organization.

3. By extension, it can refer to the general shape of a complex work—not only a building but its overall design, its visible configuration from the outside.
H4011.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to build" or "to construct." It is a derived noun: it expresses the act of construction in the sense of result, what has been built and how it is organized. Words from the same family all evoke the idea of building, erecting, and establishing a construction according to a plan.
H4011.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond, in Ezekiel 40:2. It is in a prophetic vision where Ezekiel is transported to a very high mountain and discovers "like a city built." The context shows that the prophet contemplates not the details, but the entirety of the shape and organization of this city. The term emphasizes the impression of a well-thought-out and completed architectural totality.
H4011.portee: For the reader of this passage, the word invites one to see the prophetic vision as a spectacle of coherence and beauty: a complete and orderly structure. This reinforces the idea that order and organization come from God and reveal His wisdom. It is also an invitation to contemplate the divine plan in its entirety, far beyond mere details.

sens: One of the valiant warriors of King David
H4012.detail: Mebunnaï is the name of a man who served in David's army during the united monarchy of Israel. He appears in the list of the thirty elite warriors of the king (2 Samuel 23:27), where he is presented as coming from Husha. He is a renowned fighter, recognized for his valor and dedication to the service of the king.
H4012.origine: The name Mebunnaï literally means "building of Jehovah" or "construction of the Eternal," composed of the Hebrew "ben" (to build) and the divine name. This man is also known by the alternative name Sibbechaï or Sibbecaï, indicating that he was known by several forms of his name in the ancient traditions of Israel.
H4012.emploi: Mebunnaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:27. He is listed among the thirty valiant warriors of David, a famous elite warrior group of the kingdom. Although few details are given about his personal exploits, his presence in this prestigious list attests to his recognized military value and important status at the royal court.

sens: City surrounded by defensive walls and fortifications
Military stronghold or fortified position where one takes refuge
Figuratively: what is a refuge, a protection, an unshakeable strength
H4013.detail:
1. A fortress is a city or position surrounded by high walls, towers, and defenses to withstand attacks. When the Israelites explore Canaan, they ask if the cities are "fortified" (Numbers 13:19): this is a crucial detail, as it means they are dangerous to conquer. Similarly, during the fall of Jerusalem, Jeremiah lists the strong cities that continue to resist: Lachish and Azekah (Jeremiah 34:7).
2. The word also refers to any stronghold or fortified place where one can defend oneself or take shelter. The Philistines possessed several of these strongholds (1 Samuel 6:18), and Gideon is commanded to "destroy the altar of Baal and the fence beside it" (which implies fortified places, Judges 6).
3. Figuratively, a fortress becomes an image of what protects, what is solid and unshakeable. Jeremiah receives this promise from God: "I have made you like a fortress" (Jeremiah 1:18), to signify that God makes him unmovable and strong in the face of opposition. It is the quiet strength of divine refuge.
H4013.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to enclose, to fortify." This root evokes the idea of providing shelter by building an enclosure. The word belongs to the family of words related to defense and security. It regularly appears in the Old Testament to speak of fortified cities in the ancient Near East, where the wall was the fundamental element of urban security.
H4013.emploi: This word appears 37 times in the Old Testament, especially in the historical and prophetic books. It describes the fortified cities of Canaan that the Israelites must conquer (Numbers 13:19, 32:17), and it frequently recurs in accounts of wars and sieges (2 Kings 18:8, Jeremiah 34:7, Daniel 11:39). Isaiah and Jeremiah use it to announce the destruction of enemy cities (Isaiah 34:13, Jeremiah 5:17). Finally, figuratively, it personifies what is unshakeable: Jeremiah receives from God the status of fortress against his enemies (Jeremiah 1:18), an image of God's strength itself.
H4013.portee: This word teaches us that true strength does not primarily reside in the walls and weapons of this world, but in the protection of God. When the text speaks of destroying fortresses, it shows that no human defense withstands divine will. For the believer, God becomes our "fortress"—an unshakeable refuge when everything collapses around us.

sens: Edomite chief from the patriarchal period
H4014.detail: Mibtsar is one of the chiefs or princes of Edom mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Esau. The name appears twice in the Bible, in nearly identical lists of Edomite chiefs.
H4014.origine: The name Mibtsar literally means "fortress" in Hebrew, derived from the root that evokes a fortified place or stronghold. It is a place name that became a personal name, probably because it designated a chief who resided or governed from a fortress. Like many Edomite names, this name reflects the geography and political structure of the territories of Edom.
H4014.emploi: Mibtsar is mentioned twice in the Bible, in Genesis 36:42 and 1 Chronicles 1:53, both in enumerations of the chiefs or princes of Edom during the patriarchal times. These two passages are parallel and appear in genealogical lists that organize the descendants of Esau according to their political hierarchy. Mibtsar always appears in the same position, alongside other chiefs like Kenaz and Teman, indicating his established and recognized status among the Edomite chiefs.

sens: one who flees to escape danger
flight, escape
H4015.detail:
1. A fugitive is a person who flees, who runs to escape immediate peril. In Ezekiel 17:21, the fugitives of the king's army are those who try to escape when military disaster strikes them: they cannot stay to fight, they can only run to save their lives, and even this flight catches up with them ("they shall fall by the sword").
2. By extension, the word also evokes the act of fleeing itself, the movement of escape: not only the person, but the act of running to safety. It is the image of disorder and disaster, when the army can no longer hold its position.
H4015.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "barach" (בּרח), which means "to flee, to escape." This root paints the very concrete image of someone saving themselves by running. The form "miv.rach" adds a prefix that makes it a noun: literally "one who flees" or "act of fleeing." The same verb appears throughout the Bible to describe escapes: Noah flees the flood, Moses flees Egypt, David flees Saul. It is a word of urgent movement and danger.
H4015.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible (Ezekiel 17:21), in a passage where the prophet announces the collapse of the power of the king of Egypt and his allies. It precisely describes these soldiers who attempt to flee the battlefield: they are struck by the sword or scattered. This passage paints a picture of total helplessness: even flight cannot save one who opposes God. The term emphasizes disorder, panic, the impossibility of escape.
H4015.portee: This word reminds us that before the power of God, no escape is possible. For the Christian reader, it invites reflection: attempting to flee from God brings no security. Salvation does not come from frantic running, but from returning to God and obedience. It is a striking image of the futility of all resistance.

sens: the genital organs, the intimate parts of the body
that which causes shame or dishonor
H4016.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the male genital organs, those parts of the body that are not shown in public. This is the concrete and direct meaning: in Deuteronomy 25:11, a woman seizes a man "by the private parts" during a quarrel, an act that injures and dishonors him.
2. More broadly, the word evokes anything that causes shame or dishonor. The intimate parts are called "private" not because they are bad in themselves, but because exposing them or speaking about them publicly was considered a serious affront in biblical culture.
H4016.origine: The Hebrew word is formed from a root meaning "to be ashamed" or "to cause shame." Its literal meaning is "that which excites shame." It is a euphemistic term, as many exist in languages: rather than naming directly, one describes by the effect — shame — that this reality produces. This word reflects the mentality of ancient cultures for which the exposure of the body, especially intimate parts, represented a serious offense.
H4016.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 25:11. It is a law that prohibits a woman from seizing a man by the private parts to defend him, even if her intention is good. The context shows that this act is severely punished — the woman's hand must be cut off — because it constitutes a major outrage to the dignity and honor of the body. It is a passage that establishes the limit: even in an act of defense, there are forms of violence or humiliation that are unacceptable.
H4016.portee: This passage reminds us that the dignity of the human body is sacred in the Bible, even in situations of conflict. It teaches us that certain acts, even if they pursue an acceptable goal, cross a moral line. For the believer, this underscores the importance of respecting the integrity and dignity of others, even when defending oneself or acting with good intentions.

sens: Son of Ishmael
Descendant of Simeon
H4017G.detail:
1. Mibsam is a son of Ishmael, the son that Abraham had with Hagar. He appears in the biblical genealogies as one of the twelve sons of Ishmael listed in Genesis 25:13, alongside his brothers Nebajoth, Kedar, and others. His name literally means "sweet smell" or "pleasant fragrance" in Hebrew.
2. Another Mibsam, a descendant of the tribe of Simeon, is mentioned in later genealogies of Israel. He is listed among the heads of Simeonite families during the Old Testament period.
H4017G.origine: The name Mibsam comes from two Hebrew words: *miv* ("of") and *besem* ("balsam, perfume"). This composition evokes a pleasant smell, probably a perfume or aromatic balm. Among his brothers, some also bear names of Semitic origin: Nebajoth, Kedar, Tema denote Arab peoples or desert regions. The name may reflect a valued quality or a paternal blessing.
H4017G.emploi: Mibsam is mentioned twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists. First in Genesis 25:13, where Moses lists the sons of Ishmael born to his wife Hagar, thus establishing Abraham's lineage through the Ishmaelite line. The same passage is repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:29, which reproduces this genealogy for the posterity of Israel. These two occurrences are genealogical documents without a particular narrative related to Mibsam himself; he merely appears in the list of ancestors of the Arab peoples.

sens: man of the tribe of Simeon during the divided monarchy
H4017H.detail: Mibsam is a descendant of Simeon, son of Shallum and father of Mishma, living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel (1 Chronicles 4:25). He appears in the genealogy of Simeon, one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
H4017H.origine: The name Mibsam literally means "sweet smell" or "pleasant fragrance" (from the Hebrew "besem," perfume). It is a auspicious name, common in ancient Israel to express the qualities or hopes attached to the child.
H4017H.emploi: Mibsam appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:25, in the genealogical list of the tribe of Simeon. He is presented as the son of Shallum and the father of Mishma, occupying a defined place in the succession of generations of this tribe.

sens: place where food is cooked
structure or arrangement used for cooking
H4018.detail:
1. The word refers to a hearth, that is, a place where food is cooked, a cooking area. In the vision of the temple that Ezekiel receives, hearths are made in the walls to prepare the sacrifices and meals of the temple (Ezekiel 46:23).
2. More broadly, it refers to small structures or arrangements built to allow cooking. These hearths built into the lower part of the wall were used to cook the offerings that the priests had to prepare according to the temple rules.
H4018.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to boil" or "to cook." It concretely designates the places where food is prepared by heat. It is a practical and concrete term that refers to the daily activity of cooking.
H4018.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 46:23. It is part of the detailed description that the prophet Ezekiel receives in vision of the future temple and its arrangements. These hearths are part of the practical installations of the temple, intended for the concrete tasks of preparing sacrifices and food offered to God.
H4018.portee: This small but precise architectural detail of the future temple reminds us that God is interested in the practical details of life. The hearths of the temple symbolize the idea that even ordinary acts like preparing food can be sanctified when they serve worship and community before God.

sens: Head of a family among the exiles who returned to Jerusalem
H4019.detail: Magbisch is a proper name that designates a family head in the list of exiles from Babylon who returned to Jerusalem after the decree of Cyrus. His name appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 2:30, where it is mentioned that one hundred fifty-six men from his family returned from exile.
H4019.origine: The name Magbisch literally means "the one who gathers" or "the one who unites." It evokes the idea of gathering or assembly, which is particularly fitting for a clan leader whose role was to lead his family during the long journey back from Babylon.
H4019.emploi: Magbisch appears in the genealogical list of Ezra 2 (also repeated in Nehemiah 7), which enumerates the families and clans of the Judeans who returned from captivity under the leadership of Zerubbabel, around 538 B.C. His name and that of his descendants (one hundred fifty-six people) symbolize the restoration of God's people and the reestablishment of social and familial order in Judah after seventy years of exile.

sens: To twist threads or cords by crossing them to make a braid or cord
To create a woven or braided object in this way
H4020.detail:
1. To braid means to twist together threads, hair, or cords by regularly crossing them to create a solid and ornate braid or cord. The word evokes the image of the meticulous and repeated work of braiding: one takes several elements and interlaces them to form a single, compact, and decorative piece. In Exodus 28:14, it refers to braiding pure gold into cords to make the ornament of the high priest's breastplate.
2. By extension, to braid refers to the action of creating a finished object using this technique: the braided cord is the result of the work. It is a craftsman's work, precise and deliberate, requiring skill.
H4020.origine: The Hebrew word מִגְבָּלֹת (migbalot) comes from the root גבל which essentially means to turn, wrap, or twist. This same root evokes the idea of limitation or boundary (גָּבוּל, gavul), as a boundary marks a turn or contour. The word here retains the original sense of turning or wrapping: to braid is to wrap together elements to form a cord.
H4020.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 28:14. It describes the fine craftsmanship of the Israelite high priest: Moses commands to braid pure gold chains that will be attached to the mounts of the breastplate, the sacred ornament of the high priest. This context shows that it is a work of a skilled artisan, done under divine command for worship.
H4020.portee: This word reminds the reader of the beauty and precision of the worship required by God. Braiding is a patient and repeated work, an image of the faithfulness and excellence that God demands from His people in divine service. Even the material details of the sanctuary carry spiritual significance.

sens: Headwear worn by the priests of Israel's worship
Piece of fabric wrapped or fitted on the head
H4021.detail:
1. The bonnet is a headwear that the sons of Aaron, the priests of the temple, were to wear as part of their official attire. It is an element of their sacred clothing, marking their dignity and special role in worship (Exodus 28:40). When Moses dressed them in their priestly garments at the time of their consecration, he placed these bonnets on their heads (Leviticus 8:13).
2. The bonnet is a piece of fine fabric that wraps or fits on the head to cover it. The Bible specifies that it was made of fine linen (Exodus 39:28), just like the tunic and the belt that made up the priest's uniform. Thus, it was a quality garment, not a simple ordinary headwear, but a crafted piece that was part of the adornment of divine service.
H4021.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of girding or wrapping. It is a typical garment of the ancient Near East, worn by people of high rank or invested with a function. In Israelite religious terminology, this bonnet clearly distinguished the priests from the rest of the people.
H4021.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Bible, all in descriptions of priestly garments: twice in the instructions given to Moses for making the priest's attire (Exodus 28:40 and 29:9), once in the list of garments actually made (Exodus 39:28), and once during the actual consecration of the priests (Leviticus 8:13). In all cases, it refers to the same object: an official piece of the priestly uniform, systematically associated with the tunic and the belt.
H4021.portee: The priestly bonnet reminds the reader that worship directed to God requires a certain nobility and seriousness. The priest's clothing was not trivial: each piece, including this headwear, was designed to show that the one who presented themselves before God was set apart for a holy function. This invites the reader to reflect on the dignity of divine service and the importance of the order established by God for His worship.

sens: What is of the best quality, of the highest price
The most precious productions of a land or garden
What surpasses others in value or beauty
H4022.detail: 1. The word designates what surpasses in quality or importance. In Moses' blessings on Joseph, it names the "best fruit" of the sun and the "best products" of the land — what nature offers that is richest and most abundant (Deuteronomy 33:14-16). 2. Concretely, it evokes the agricultural treasures of a country: succulent fruits, generous harvests, gifts from heaven like rain. It is the image of a divine blessing materializing His favor. 3. Figuratively, it qualifies what is sought after, coveted for its rarity or beauty: in the Song of Songs, the "excellent fruits" of the beloved garden symbolize the desirable and precious intimacy (Song of Songs 4:13, 4:16).
H4022.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be excellent" or "to surpass." It is close to verbs expressing superiority or distinction. The concept is rooted in concrete observation: what is "better" is seen, recognized by its manifest quality.
H4022.emploi: The word appears seven times, primarily in the blessing of Joseph (Deuteronomy 33:13-16), where Moses enumerates the material blessings that God reserves for this tribe — dew, sun, harvests, mountains. It reappears in the Song of Songs (4:13, 4:16, 7:14) to describe the delights of the garden and the fruits of the beloved, where excellence takes on both sensual and spiritual dimensions. The context is always one of abundance, divine blessing, or desire.
H4022.portee: This word teaches us that God blesses His servants not only with spiritual goods but with concrete material gifts. He values creation and its fruits as signs of divine favor. For the Christian, it reminds us that good things — health, family, sustenance — are not distractions, but legitimate forms of God's blessing.

sens: Ancient fortified city of Canaan
Site of significant battles in the history of Israel
Valley where decisive combats took place
H4023.detail: Megiddo is an ancient city in the territory of Canaan, assigned to the tribe of Manasseh. It was located on the southern edge of the Plain of Jezreel (now part of Galilee), near Mount Carmel. This strategic geographical position made it an essential passage point and a major military objective. The city is mentioned during the conquest of the territory by Joshua and later remains a royal power center: it is among the fortified cities that King Solomon reorganized (1 Kings 4:12, 9:15). Megiddo is especially famous as a battlefield: it is where King Ahaziah of Judah was mortally wounded while fleeing from the Israelite king Jehu (2 Kings 9:27), and it is in the valley of Megiddo that King Josiah was killed fighting against Pharaoh Necho (2 Chronicles 35:22). The name itself means "place of crowds," likely evoking the military gatherings and battles that took place there. The city gave its name to Armageddon, the symbolic site of final judgment in Revelation.
H4023.origine: The Hebrew name Megiddo literally means "place of crowds" or "place of gatherings," composed of megud ("crowd," "gathering") and the locative suffix -o. The city bears this name due to its position in a plain that hosted large troop movements and armies. In the Greek New Testament, Megiddo is referred to as Armageddon (Ἀρμαγεδδών), a direct transliteration of the Hebrew name that designates the site of the eschatological battle of the Last Judgment in Revelation.
H4023.emploi: Megiddo appears twelve times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of Joshua, Judges, Kings, and Chronicles. The city is first mentioned as a stronghold to be conquered during Israel's establishment in Canaan (Joshua 12:21, 17:11; Judges 1:27). It later becomes an important royal possession under Solomon, integrated into the supply and defense systems of the kingdom (1 Kings 4:12; 1 Kings 9:15). Megiddo also serves as the setting for two major royal dramas: the flight and death of Ahaziah king of Judah (2 Kings 9:27; 2 Kings 23:29-30) and the death in battle of King Josiah against the Egyptian armies (2 Chronicles 35:22). This accumulation of tragic and warlike moments has marked biblical memory and contributed to making it the apocalyptic symbol of Armageddon.
H4023.portee: Megiddo reminds the Christian reader of God's sovereignty over history and political events. Although strategically well-placed and militarily significant, the city never ensured lasting security for Israel: the kings who controlled it or fought at its gates experienced defeats and death. Its mention in Revelation under the name Armageddon emphasizes that true judgment and true victory belong to God alone, not to human forces.

sens: tall structure made of stone or wood serving as a fortress or lookout
defensive building in a fortified city
protective refuge
H4024A.detail: 1. A tower is a tall and sturdy construction, made of stone or wood, built to dominate a territory, monitor approaches, or serve as a military stronghold. In Jericho, the walls had towers (Joshua 2:15). 2. It is the central element of fortified cities in biblical times: each enclosure relied on several watch and combat towers, from which watchers could see the enemy coming from afar. 3. Figuratively, the tower represents strength, security, protection — the place where one finds refuge when everything collapses. This is why Psalm 61:4 says, "You will be for me a refuge, a strong tower": God is compared to a tower because He is unshakeable and protective.
H4024A.origine: The Hebrew word גּדוֹל (gadol) means "great"; mig-dol thus literally means "a great [edifice]." It is the same word that appears in Migdol, the name of a fortress in Egypt (Exodus 14:2). The root evokes the idea of something that stands high, of what is elevated and imposing.
H4024A.emploi: The word tower appears about twenty times in the Bible. It is first encountered in historical accounts to describe the fortifications of cities: Jericho, Hebron, the walls of Jerusalem. It also appears in poetic texts and psalms, where it takes on a spiritual dimension: God is called "tower of salvation" (2 Samuel 22:51 says, "He grants great deliverances to His king"), refuge of the righteous against their enemies. This passage shows that God's tower is the source of royal security — it is an image of the solidity of His protection.
H4024A.portee: Understanding that God is compared to a tower reminds us that our faith rests on an unshakeable foundation. When life threatens us or when we are besieged, God is not fragile or distant — He is like an impregnable fortress. This image invites the believer to seek refuge not in human defenses, but in the presence and strength of God.

sens: fortified city in the northeast of Egypt, near the border
region where Jews exiled after the fall of Jerusalem
H4024B.detail: 1. Migdol is a fortified city located in the northeast of Egypt, near the Mediterranean Sea and the border with Sinai. It is mentioned as a geographical landmark: during the Exodus, Israel camps "before Migdol" and "the sea" (Exodus 14:2), between the city and Baal-Zephon, at the time when Pharaoh pursues them. Ezekiel also uses Migdol as a territorial boundary of Egypt, naming it with Syene to designate the whole country "from Migdol to Syene" (Ezekiel 29:10). 2. After the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., a group of surviving Jews takes refuge in Egypt, notably in Migdol (Jeremiah 44:1). Jeremiah warns them that even in this distant place, the sword of divine judgment will reach them (Jeremiah 46:14), for fleeing from God's will offers no protection.
H4024B.origine: The name Migdol comes from ancient Hebrew and literally means "tower" (migdal). It was indeed a fortification with watchtowers, a strategic place commanding the trade and military routes of northeastern Egypt. The word is of Semitic origin, like many place names in ancient Egypt where Near Eastern populations lived.
H4024B.emploi: Migdol appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the context of Egypt. Three occurrences concern the Exodus and the forty years in the desert: it serves as a geographical marker to locate Israel's camp at the time of the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:2, Numbers 33:7). Three other occurrences relate to the prophecies of Jeremiah and Ezekiel against Egypt: it marks the northern boundary of the Egyptian country and hosts Jewish refugees after 586 B.C. (Jeremiah 44:1, 46:14). Ezekiel invokes it as a landmark to announce the future devastation of Egypt (Ezekiel 29:10, 30:6).
H4024B.portee: Migdol reminds us that even the most distant places, even exile, remain under God's watch and judgment. The Jews fleeing to Egypt, far from the temple and Jerusalem, do not find refuge in human powers: God hears Jeremiah's warnings even to Migdol, to the borders of the known world. It is a lesson in humility: geographical distance does not deliver from divine judgment when one strays from His Word.

sens: Chief of Edom, descendant of Esau
H4025.detail: Magdiel is one of the tribal chiefs of Edom listed in the genealogy of the descendants of Esau. The name means "prince of God" in Hebrew. It appears in the genealogical lists of Genesis 36:43 and 1 Chronicles 1:54, where it is presented among the chiefs of Edom governing their respective territories.
H4025.origine: The name Magdiel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "mag" (chief, prince) and "diel" (God). It thus literally means "prince of God." This name reflects the biblical custom of giving children theophoric names expressing a relationship to God.
H4025.emploi: Magdiel is mentioned twice in the Bible, solely in the genealogies of Edom. In Genesis 36:43, he appears in the list of Edomite chiefs with their dwellings, establishing the descendants of Esau as distinct peoples. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 1:54 repeats this same genealogy exactly. Magdiel is presented as a chief of Edomite district, holding a place of power among the tribes of Edom.

sens: fortified defensive structure, tall and robust, intended to watch over and protect a city or its boundaries
H4026G.detail: 1. A tower is a tall vertical structure, usually made of stone, that served to monitor the approaches to a city and defend it. It also marked a visible landmark from afar. In the three provided passages, the tower of Hananeel is mentioned as a specific geographical point at the northern gates of Jerusalem, serving as a boundary or landmark during the reconstruction of the city after the exile (Nehemiah 12:39; Jeremiah 31:38; Zechariah 14:10).
H4026G.origine: The Hebrew word migdal (מִגְדָּל) comes from a root that evokes the idea of rising up, becoming great. It is a concrete word: a tower is something visible, massive, that dominates the landscape. The word frequently appears in the Old Testament to designate various defensive towers, watchtowers, or towers around fortified cities.
H4026G.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided passages, all related to Jerusalem and its boundaries. The tower of Hananeel (‘grace of God’) was a defensive structure located northeast of the old city. It is mentioned at three points: during the reconstruction project under Nehemiah after the exile (Nehemiah 12:39), in Jeremiah's prophetic promise about the restoration of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 31:38), and in Zechariah's eschatological vision of glorified Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:10). Each time, it serves as a geographical landmark to delineate the city or the territory that will be restored.
H4026G.portee: The tower of Hananeel is a symbol of stability and divine protection. Its very name, ‘grace of God,’ suggests that the defense of Jerusalem rests on the favor of the Lord. For the reader, this tower reminds us that the promises of restoration and divine blessing come with a concrete reality: God visibly and tangibly restores His city, not just in promise.

sens: Tall construction intended for the surveillance or defense of a city
Building serving as a fortified refuge
Figuratively: protection, strength, or power
H4026H.detail:
1. A tower is a tall and robust construction built to allow those who ascend it to monitor the surroundings and defend a city. In Nehemiah 3:1, the ‘tower of Meah’ is part of the fortifications of Jerusalem, built as an element of the wall defense system — it is a strategic point of the wall that the Jewish people restore after the exile.

2. Beyond its military role, a tower can also serve as a refuge where one can take shelter in times of danger. It then represents a safe and fortified place, a bastion to which one can confide.

3. In a more spiritual or figurative sense, the tower becomes an image of strength, protection, and power — a source of security and trust for those who find refuge there.
H4026H.origine: The Hebrew word מִגְדָּל (migdal) comes from a root that expresses the idea of rising or growing. In biblical times, towers were common structures in fortified cities of the Near East: they served both as military observation points and as refuges. The term is used for any tall construction, whether civil, military, or religious. It is a very ancient word, rooted in the concrete life of the cities of the Levant.
H4026H.emploi: The word מִגְדָּל appears only once in the provided usage: Nehemiah 3:1, where it designates the ‘tower of Meah,’ one of the restored elements of the fortifications of Jerusalem. The term here is concrete and architectural: it refers to a real part of the city wall, a defensive structure that the builders erect or repair after the return from exile. The use of the word reminds us that the reconstruction of Jerusalem involves the restoration of its defensive, material, and symbolic structures. The historical context of the book of Nehemiah (restoration of the walls in the 5th century B.C.) shows that towers were essential to the security and integrity of an ancient city.
H4026H.portee: For the reader, this tower reminds us that the protection of a city — and by extension, that of a people — rests on tangible structures, built with effort and dedication. The act of Nehemiah and the builders expresses the people's desire to rebuild themselves, physically and spiritually, after the exile. This reconstruction of the fortifications becomes a sign of God's return to His people and the restoration of their dignity.

sens: tall construction made of stone or brick, generally round or square in shape, serving as fortification or surveillance
step or level of a structure
H4026I.detail:
1. The tower is a robust and imposing construction, built high to dominate a region and protect it. In Nehemiah 3:11, we see the ‘tower of the ovens’ being restored in the rebuilt walls of Jerusalem: it is a specific tower that served to monitor or defend a particular part of the wall, near artisan areas or public kitchens. This tower was part of the city's fortification system.
2. The word can also refer to a step or level of a tall structure, such as the different floors of a steeple tower or a distinct level in a high construction.
H4026I.origine: The Hebrew word מִגְדָּל (migdal) comes from a root that evokes the idea of greatness and elevation. It appears very often in the Hebrew Bible to designate watchtowers, fortified towers, and defensive structures. The word belongs to a family of terms related to height and spatial dominance. It is a simple and concrete word that primarily describes the architectural object before any metaphorical use.
H4026I.emploi: The word מִגְדָּל appears only once in this passage from the book of Nehemiah to designate the ‘tower of the ovens.’ Nehemiah describes the meticulous reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile, section by section. This specific tower, named because it was located near the city’s ovens, was a key defensive element of the rampart. Its restoration was among the essential works to consolidate the defenses of the holy city.
H4026I.portee: This mention of the tower of the ovens reminds us that the protection and construction of a city require order, clarity in tasks, and visible cooperation from everyone. For a Christian reader, the reconstruction of Jerusalem under Nehemiah symbolizes the restoration of what has been ruined and the commitment of each individual in this common work, like the stones of a spiritual edifice.

sens: Tall structure made of stone or brick, generally square or round, intended for defense or surveillance
Raised part of a wall or fortification, serving as a lookout and combat post
Small building or platform used for gatherings or as a place of refuge
Poetic image of something strong, stable, or beautiful
H4026M.detail:
1. A tower is a tall building, generally constructed to monitor or defend the surrounding territory. In Babylon, the people wanted to build "a tower whose top reaches to heaven" (Genesis 11:4), symbolizing their ambition. Towers were part of city defenses: in Jerusalem, Hezekiah "raised it up to the towers" (2 Chronicles 32:5), thus reinforcing the protection of his capital.
2. On the walls of fortified cities, towers were built to see the enemy approaching from afar and to defend. In Shechem, the inhabitants took refuge "in the tower of Shechem" (Judges 9:49) when danger approached. These constructions were strategic strong points of the ramparts.
3. A platform or elevated place where people in authority stand. Nehemiah stands on "the platform" (Nehemiah 8:4) to read the Law to the people. It is also an elevated bed in the garden (Isaiah 5:2).
4. In poetry, a tower becomes the image of strength and beauty: the psalmist calls God his "strong tower" (Psalms 61:4), as it symbolizes protection and stability; the Song of Solomon compares the neck and nose of the beloved to towers (Song of Solomon 7:5), both for their elegance and nobility.
H4026M.origine: The Hebrew word "migdal" comes from a root that expresses the idea of "to rise" or "to ascend." The word naturally evokes something that rises, that elevates above the ground. In the Bible, towers were everywhere — cities of the Levant, such as Jerusalem or Jericho, had them marking the corners of their walls. The word is also used to refer to any elevated structure intended for the control or contemplation of a vast space.
H4026M.emploi: This word appears 39 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives (Kings, Chronicles), descriptions of restored Jerusalem (Nehemiah), and poetry (Psalms, Song of Solomon, Isaiah). In historical contexts, towers are elements of fortification: Hezekiah builds them to defend Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:5), Uzziah builds them in the wilderness (2 Chronicles 26:10). In poetry, particularly in the Song of Solomon and Psalms, the tower becomes an image of strength, beauty, and spiritual refuge. The word also applies to small structures: a platform to speak to the people (Nehemiah 8:4) or an elevated bed in the garden (Isaiah 5:2). This range of uses shows that the word designates any elevated construction, from a simple podium to a large fortification tower.
H4026M.portee: The word "tower" in the Bible invites the reader to reflect on what makes us strong and keeps us safe. God is called a "tower" by the psalmist, which means He lifts us above danger and gives us a clear view of our enemies. For the Christian faith, this language reminds us that our true protection does not come from our material defenses, but from the One who keeps us. Understanding this biblical image enriches our reading of prayers and hymns that compare trust in God to an unshakeable refuge or fortress.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Naphtali
H4027.detail: 1. Migdal-El is a fortified city that belonged to the territory assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the Promised Land (Joshua 19:38). Its Hebrew name literally means "tower of God," evoking a defensive structure erected as a landmark or refuge.
H4027.origine: The name Migdal-El is composed of two Hebrew elements: "migdal" meaning "tower" or "fortress," and "El" referring to God. It is a common place name in Israel, reflecting either the presence of a defensive structure or a religious consecration of the site.
H4027.emploi: Migdal-El is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:38, in the list of cities assigned to Naphtali during the division of the Promised Land by Joshua. It appears among a series of nineteen cities with their villages. Ancient translations, including the Segond, refer to it as Horem, suggesting that the ancient site bore several names over time.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Judah in antiquity
H4028.detail: Migdal-Gad is a fortified city that belonged to the territory assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of Canaan. Its name means "tower of God" in Hebrew, evoking an elevated defensive structure. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities of Judah established in Joshua 15:37, between Zaanan and Hadashah.
H4028.origine: The name Migdal-Gad is composed of two Hebrew words: "migdal" (מִגְדַּל) meaning "tower" or "fortress," and "Gad" (גַּד) meaning "God." This type of double name, associating a geographical term with a divine reference, was common in Canaan to designate important or sacred places. The name reflects the military or religious significance of the site in antiquity.
H4028.emploi: Migdal-Gad appears only in Joshua 15:37, in the systematic enumeration of fortified cities in the territory of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. This administrative list establishes the boundaries and possessions of each tribe. The exact site of this city has not been definitively identified by modern archaeologists, but its inclusion in this list shows that it was a recognized stronghold in southern Canaan.

sens: Shepherd's tower located near Bethlehem, serving as a refuge and lookout for flocks
H4029.detail: Migdal-Éder is a tower built in the region of Bethlehem, specifically constructed for shepherds to monitor and protect their flocks of sheep. Its name literally means "tower of the flock." It was a fortified structure serving both as a refuge against wild animals and as a strategic observation point. In Genesis 35:21, Jacob sets up his tent there after stopping in the region of Bethlehem, indicating that it was a well-known and recognizable place. The prophet Micah (4:8) refers to it as a symbolic geographical landmark of the kingdom of Judah.
H4029.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew words: "migdal" (מִגְדַּל) meaning "tower" or "fortress," and "eder" (עֵדֶר) meaning "flock" or "shepherd." It is an ancient geographical name, particular to the region of Bethlehem, designating a real structure intended for pastoral life.
H4029.emploi: Migdal-Éder is mentioned twice in the Bible. First in Genesis 35:21, where Jacob establishes his camp after leaving Bethel, marking a moment in his life during his travels in Canaan. Then in Micah 4:8, the prophet alludes to it symbolically to speak of the return of royal power to Jerusalem, using this tower as an image of the kingdom and the restoration of Davidic royalty. This dual usage shows that Migdal-Éder was a concrete and memorable geographical location, also becoming a spiritual reference point for the prophets.
H4029.portee: For the Christian reader, Migdal-Éder evokes the proximity of Bethlehem, the city of David and the birthplace of Jesus. It is in the fields near Bethlehem that the shepherds watched over their flocks on the night of the Nativity, reminding us that this tower was at the heart of an important pastoral region. It brings to mind the pastoral vocation of King David himself, who tended his father's sheep before being called to shepherd Israel.

sens: A valuable present offered to someone
A rare or cherished object to possess
What enriches or honors the recipient
H4030.detail:
1. The word designates a gift, a present given to honor or gratify someone. It is a gift of value — not just any object, but something esteemed. When Abraham's servant gives "rich gifts" to Rebekah and her family (Genesis 24:53), he offers silver, gold, and clothing to show the importance of his master and his request.
2. It is also a cherished, rare, or remarkable object due to its quality. The "precious items" that the king gives to his sons (2 Chronicles 21:3) or that the peoples bring to Jerusalem (Ezra 1:6) are not ordinary goods, but things worthy of esteem. The word emphasizes what shines through its rarity or excellence.
3. More broadly, it is what enriches the recipient — both materially and socially. Receiving such a gift is to be honored and regarded.
H4030.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be great" or "to rise." It is linked to the idea of size, elevation, and thus importance and value. A gift that rises above the ordinary, that stands out due to its excellence, is a "migdana." It is a present worthy of both the giver and the receiver.
H4030.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe significant gifts. In Genesis 24:53, it is a pledge of covenant and respect. In the passages from Chronicles and Ezra, it refers to gifts from kings or peoples — items given during significant events (sharing of the kingdom, restoration of the Temple). Each time, the context is one of royal generosity or solemn offering. The term always emphasizes the quality and weight of the gift, never just its quantity.
H4030.portee: This word reminds us that giving, in the Bible, is not a trivial act. Offering a precious gift is to acknowledge the other, seal a covenant, and show respect. For the Christian reader, it can evoke the meaning of true generosity: not giving just anything, but giving what costs and honors. It is also a subtle image of God's gifts — not ordinary objects, but presents worthy of His love.

sens: Son of Japheth and grandson of Noah
Mountainous region in the north, inhabited by the descendants of Magog
H4031G.detail:
1. Magog is a character from biblical antiquity: the second son of Japheth and grandson of Noah (Genesis 10:2). He is listed among the ancestors of peoples who dispersed after the flood. His name literally means "land of Gog."

2. By extension, Magog also designates the mountainous region and the peoples descended from this son of Japheth. This land, located between Cappadocia and Media, north of Israel, was inhabited by tribes from his lineage. It is a region of the ancient known world, often associated with distant northern peoples.
H4031G.origine: The name Magog comes from a Semitic root and means "land of Gog." In the Table of Nations in Genesis 10, Magog is listed among the descendants of Japheth, one of Noah's three sons. The same Magog appears in 1 Chronicles 1:5, confirming his place in the biblical genealogy. His name has remained attached to the region that his descendants would have occupied, becoming a geographical term to designate the lands of the distant North.
H4031G.emploi: Magog appears twice in the French Old Testament of the Segond: in the Table of Nations in Genesis 10:2, where he is listed as the second son of Japheth, and in 1 Chronicles 1:5, which repeats the same genealogy. These two passages are lists of peoples and regions after the flood, showing how humanity dispersed. Magog thus represents one of the three major branches of Noah's descendants and the lands associated with his descendants.
H4031G.portee: Magog reminds the reader that all peoples, even the most distant and least known of the ancient world, are descended from humanity created by God and saved by Noah. It is an invitation to recognize the unity of humankind and the divine providence that guides the history of all peoples, both near and far.

sens: Mountainous region between Cappadocia and Media
People or power hostile to Israel in eschatological times
H4031H.detail:
1. Magog designates a mountainous region located between Cappadocia (southeast of present-day Asia Minor) and Media (northwest of present-day Iran). It is the territory traditionally inhabited by the descendants of Magog, son of Japheth and grandson of Noah according to the genealogy of nations in Genesis 10.

2. In the prophecy of Ezekiel, Magog represents an enemy power of Israel that will rise in the last days. Gog, the prince of Magog, gathers allies (Rosh, Meshech, Tubal) for a massive invasion against Israel, which the Lord will destroy by fire (Ezekiel 38:2; 39:6).
H4031H.origine: The name literally means "land of Gog." Magog is first a man, son of Japheth, ancestor of a people (Genesis 10:2). His Hebrew name is linked to that of Gog, whose origin remains obscure — perhaps a variant of "gag" meaning "roof" or "height." In the biblical tradition, Magog embodies a distant, mountainous, and potentially hostile people, evoking regions of the north and northeast of the world known to the Hebrews.
H4031H.emploi: Magog appears only twice in the Bible, exclusively in the prophecies of Ezekiel (chapters 38-39). These two verses form a coherent prophetic block: in Ezekiel 38:2, Magog is the territory of prince Gog, from which an eschatological invasion against Israel will arise; in Ezekiel 39:6, the Lord sends fire into Magog and the islands (the distant lands of the diaspora) to demonstrate His power. The term retains a dual meaning here: it is both a real geographical place (or supposed to be) and an apocalyptic symbol of organized rebellion against God's people in the last days.
H4031H.portee: These prophecies about Magog teach believers that the Lord controls history and the powers of the world until the last days. Even the most distant and powerful nations cannot shake God's plan or defeat Israel: He alone judges and delivers. This text invites the reader to an unwavering trust in God's sovereignty, beyond apparent threats.

sens: Fear, terror, fright in the face of danger
Misfortune, mishap, that which causes fear
Granary, place for storing harvests
H4035.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes physical fear, the dread that a threat provokes. In Isaiah 66:4, God says He will take pleasure in the misfortune of those who disobey Him, meaning He will allow what terrifies and overwhelms them to come upon them.
2. By extension, it also signifies the misfortune itself, the unfortunate situation that one fears — less the feeling than its real cause. The context of Isaiah clearly shows that misfortune is not just an emotion, but a concrete calamity sent as judgment.
3. In a completely different usage (Haggai 2:19), the same Hebrew word means granary, the place where one gathers and stores the harvest. This meaning is likely explained by the ancient idea that the granary is a place where one "contains" or "holds" the grains — an image of confinement or custody that recalls the fear that "holds" a person.
H4035.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of limit, enclosure, or confinement. In the family of the word, there is the idea of "shelter" or "refuge." The dual meaning — fear and granary — rests on this image of something enclosed or retained: fear paralyzes and confines a person, while the granary holds provisions. It is a specifically Hebrew word.
H4035.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 66:4, it denotes the misfortune and terror that God sends as judgment upon those who despise Him — it is a word of threat and divine justice. In Haggai 2:19, it literally means granary or silo, in an oracle where God announces that before this day the granaries were empty, but from now on He will pour out His blessing. The two usages are distinct: one pertains to divine judgment, the other to agricultural economy and blessing.
H4035.portee: This word reminds us that the fear of misfortune is a reality that God knows and judges. For the believer, it invites not to despise the divine word, for whoever refuses to listen will find what they dread. On the other hand, the granary would evoke for an agricultural reader abundance and order of creation — the place where God gathers His gifts.

sens: Prophetic nickname meaning "the terror on every side"
The name that the prophet Jeremiah gives to Pashur after being mistreated by him
H4036.detail: 1. Magor-Missabib literally means "the terror on every side" or "the fear that surrounds from all sides." It is a very evocative prophetic nickname: it paints the image of a person surrounded by danger and dread, with no escape. 2. In Jeremiah 20:3, after Pashur (a priest) strikes Jeremiah and puts him in stocks for denouncing the idolatry of Jerusalem, Jeremiah pronounces this nickname as a prophetic judgment: God gives Pashur this new name to announce that terror will envelop him and his family because of his hostility to the divine message.
H4036.origine: The Hebrew name "Magor-Missabib" is composed of two words: "magor" (fear, terror) and "missabib" (from all sides, around). It is an entirely prophetic name, created by Jeremiah to express God's judgment. It reflects a recurring theme in Jeremiah's preaching: those who oppose God and persecute His prophets will themselves suffer terror and desolation.
H4036.emploi: Magor-Missabib appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 20:3. It is the prophetic nickname that Jeremiah imposes on Pashur after enduring his violence. Pashur was a powerful priest who rejected Jeremiah's message; by giving him this name of misfortune, Jeremiah announces that God will turn his power and security into terror, and that his own wickedness will fall back upon him and his household. This nickname illustrates the role of the prophet who, in God's name, pronounces judgment on those who persecute the divine messenger.
H4036.portee: This passage invites the believer to reflect on the spiritual consequences of opposing God and His prophets. It shows that the persecution of God's servants does not escape divine justice: whoever does evil for having rejected God's word will have to answer for it. It is also a comfort for persecuted Christians: God does not abandon them, and He will bring justice to those who oppress them.

sens: Tool for work or war consisting of a sharp blade fixed to a handle
Instrument used for cutting, chopping, or felling
In a figurative sense, authority or power that decides matters
H4037.detail:
1. The axe is a tool composed of a sharpened metal blade attached to a long wooden handle. It is a practical instrument for splitting wood, felling trees, or for construction. In 2 Samuel 12:31, the inhabitants are subjected to various forced labors "under iron axes," meaning they must wield this tool in hard and servile work.
2. The axe is also a fearsome weapon in battle, capable of striking with force and cutting. Its use in the wars of the Old Testament illustrates the destructive power it represents.
3. In a more abstract or symbolic sense, the axe can represent God's judgment that cuts and decides the fate of nations or individuals.
H4037.origine: The Hebrew word מַגְזֵרָה (magzérah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of "cutting" or "chopping." This term belongs to the family of Hebrew words related to separation and division. Its basic image is the action of cutting cleanly, which explains why it is applied to this quintessential cutting tool that is the axe.
H4037.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 12:31. It is a specialized term for the iron axe used in the forced labor imposed on the inhabitants of the Ammonite cities after David's military victory. The context shows the use of the axe as an instrument of labor in a setting of servitude, mixed with other tools like saws and harrows. It is a rare word, perhaps more literary or less common than other Hebrew terms for axe.
H4037.portee: This passage reveals the harshness of the fate imposed on the defeated peoples in the Old Testament: the inhabitants must perform hard labor with iron tools under military domination. It is a reminder that earthly power, even victorious, carries a dark side of suffering and servitude.

sens: Agricultural tool with a curved blade for cutting grains and harvests
Signal that the time for divine judgment has come
H4038.detail:
1. The sickle is the cutting tool that harvesters hold in hand to cut the stalks of wheat at the base. It is the classic instrument of harvest in the ancient world: in Joel 3:13, the prophet calls to "put in the sickle" because "the harvest is ripe," showing that it is the object that accomplishes the work of gathering at the opportune moment.
2. Figuratively, the sickle becomes the image of God's judgment: when the grains are ripe, they are harvested and destroyed. Thus in Jeremiah 50:16, the order to "exterminate the one who wields the sickle" represents the annihilation of Babylon by divine judgment, with the harvest as a metaphor for punishment and end.
H4038.origine: The Hebrew word maggal comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning or bending, which perfectly corresponds to the curved shape of the blade. The sickle is the fundamental agricultural tool in Israel, as in the entire ancient Near East: its distinctive semicircular shape allowed for the quick and repetitive motion of harvesting.
H4038.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. Both usages are prophetic and symbolic: in Jeremiah 50, the sickle marks the beginning of Babylon's destruction; in Joel 3, it announces the judgment of the nations at the end of times. In both cases, the sickle does not speak of a simple agricultural harvest, but of judgment and end, as if God Himself were taking this tool to harvest humanity.
H4038.portee: The sickle reminds the reader that God controls history and that judgment comes when the time is ripe — just as a harvest cannot be delayed when the grains are ready. It is an image that is both sober and terrifying: human work of harvesting becomes the model of divine judgment, inevitable and at its appointed time.

sens: A long and narrow object rolled up on itself, usually made of papyrus or leather
A written document containing words or a law
A book or text in divine order
H4039.detail: 1. The scroll is primarily a material object: a long strip of papyrus or leather that is rolled around a stick for preservation and transport. Ezekiel sees in his vision a scroll that is written on, and he is commanded to eat it, as what is written inside must be assimilated (Ezekiel 3:2). 2. The scroll then serves as the medium for the words of God. Jeremiah dictates the words of the Lord to the scribe Baruch, who writes them on a scroll; King Jehoiakim burns this scroll, but God commands Jeremiah to fill another scroll with the same words (Jeremiah 36:21 and 36:32). The written text has authority and permanence: it is the fixed Word of God. 3. Finally, the scroll can simply refer to a book or collection. Psalm 40 affirms that the scroll of the book is written for the one who comes to do the will of God (Psalms 40:8), an image of fulfillment and destiny.
H4039.origine: The Hebrew word מְגִלָּה (megillah) comes from the root גלל (galal), which means "to roll, to wrap." A scroll is literally what is rolled. The Aramaic uses the same word.
