In the Bible, this term always refers to the rolled object with its contents, never in a state of mere material. The feminine form marks its belonging to the class of concrete and visible objects.
H4039.emploi: The word megillah appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, as well as in Psalm 40 and Zechariah. In Jeremiah 36, the account of the scroll that Jeremiah dictates to Baruch and then the king burns constitutes the most developed usage: we see the scroll written, read, brought to the king, burned, and rewritten. It is a key moment where Scripture becomes persecuted but indestructible. In Ezekiel 2:9 and 3:1-3, Ezekiel sees a scroll written, filled with lamentations and woes, and God commands him to eat it: an image of the internalization of the Word. Zechariah 5:1-2 mentions a flying scroll, a true apocalyptic vision. The word alternates with "book" (sefer), but megillah emphasizes the rolled object more, hence the choice of "scroll."
H4039.portee: The scroll reminds us that the Word of God does not exist only in spirit, but is inscribed in the concrete and in history. It can be written, transported, persecuted, but it remains indestructible: Jehoiakim burns the scroll, but God has it rewritten. For the Christian reader, this affirms that God entrusts His Word to material texts and to those who keep them. This is also why Ezekiel must eat the scroll: so that the Word does not remain external, but dwells within the one who receives it.

sens: Written document rolled up on itself, an ancient form of the book
Written text or decree recorded on a material support
H4040.detail:
1. A scroll is a document or written text that was rolled around a stick or rod, like the books of ancient times. It was the standard form of the book before the codex (the sewn pages of a modern book). In Ezra 6:2, a scroll is discovered in the archives of Media that contains the record of the royal decree — it is a true official document, rolled and preserved.
2. By extension, the word designates any text, decree, or inscription recorded in writing on a durable support. The scroll represents the authority of an established text that can be unrolled and read publicly or consulted in the archives.
H4040.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root גלל (galal), which means "to roll," "to turn." This imagery is found in other biblical terms: a scroll is literally something that rolls. The Aramaic word מְגִלָּה (megillah, or megila in biblical French) is used particularly in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which deal with documents and official decrees. This Aramaic form is common in the Aramaic sections of the Old Testament.
H4040.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Ezra 6:2, in a passage entirely in Aramaic. It refers to the scroll archived in Achmetha (Ecbatana, the capital of Media) that contained the record of Cyrus's decree allowing the reconstruction of the temple. This context shows that the scroll is an official document, a written and sealed act, preserved in the royal archives. It is a testimony to the permanence and authority of the written text in Persian administration.
H4040.portee: For the reader, this passage reminds us that God can act through the written records of men and preserve His promises in history. The scroll discovered in the royal archives becomes proof that the decree for the reconstruction of the temple had indeed existed — the written word becomes an instrument of justice and restoration. This invites the believer to see divine Providence even in the documents and records of this world.

sens: Act of stealing, ravaging a place by taking its goods
Loot, the collection of wealth taken by force
Violent desire to seize something
H4041.detail:
1. Plunder is the act of stealing and ravaging a place, taking by force the goods that are there. This is what the Babylonian warriors do as they descend upon the peoples: they come "to plunder," that is, to strip away, to take everything they can (Habakkuk 1:9).
2. Plunder also refers to the collection of wealth, prisoners, and loot amassed through this violence. The text describes the Babylonians who "gather prisoners like sand" — this human and material loot is the fruit of their plunder.
3. By extension, the word can evoke the ardent desire, the greed that drives one to plunder: the gazes of the warriors are directed "forward," fueled by this thirst for conquest and accumulation.
H4041.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root related to the idea of gathering, accumulating, or perhaps from a root expressing greed and violent desire. Its exact etymology remains uncertain, but the imagery is that of wealth piled up, accumulated through theft and violence. The Babylonian context of the book of Habakkuk (where the Chaldeans invade the Levant) sheds light on this meaning: it is the organized rapacity of a conquering army.
H4041.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Habakkuk 1:9. Habakkuk, a prophet of Judah, receives a vision of the Babylonians threatening God's people. He describes them as an army come "to plunder," driven by a devouring greed and an unyielding military organization. The context emphasizes their brutal violence: they gather prisoners "like sand," treating human beings as mere loot. This unique word encapsulates the prophetic vision of Babylon's destructive rapacity.
H4041.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of divine judgment: God allows violent and rapacious nations to execute His judgment against His unfaithful people. Habakkuk contemplates this daunting truth — that the Lord even uses the wicked to accomplish His purposes — and this drives him to seek refuge in faith in God alone (see Habakkuk 3's confession of faith). This word reinforces the urgency of repentance and trust in the Lord's ultimate justice.

sens: To hand someone over to another, to put them in their power
To entrust, to hand over to someone in complete trust
To adorn, to decorate, to embellish
H4042.detail:
1. Deliver primarily means to hand over a person or a people to the power of another, often in a context of war or victory. This is what Abram affirms: God has "delivered" his enemies into his hands, meaning He has handed them over defeated and submissive (Genesis 14:20). The word evokes the idea of yielding, of handing over power.
2. Deliver takes on a softer hue when it means to entrust something to someone with full assurance: wisdom will "adorn" you with a magnificent crown (Proverbs 4:9), it clothes you with beauty like a royal garment. This nuance emphasizes trust, a voluntary handing over.
3. In Hosea 11:8, the verb expresses divine hesitation: "Should I deliver you?" God wonders if He should deliver Ephraim to destruction, despite His parental love. This meaning aligns with the first: to hand over, to resign oneself to abandonment.
H4042.origine: The verb מָגַן comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of covering, protecting, hence taking charge of something, taking it in hand. The "piel" form we are studying intensifies this action: not only to cover or envelop, but actively to hand over, to entrust, to deliver. The word is related to verbs meaning "to shelter" or "to defend," which sheds light on its polysemy: to deliver someone is also to hand them over to protection or to fate.
H4042.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, each time with a distinct nuance. In Genesis 14:20, Abram celebrates military victory: God has "delivered" his enemies at his mercy — this is the most martial sense. In Proverbs 4:9, it refers to how Wisdom adorns or clothes those who seek her — here, "deliver" takes on the meaning of "to gratify," "to provide for." In Hosea 11:8, it concerns the issue of divine judgment: God hesitates to deliver Israel to the destruction it deserves, so great is His fatherly love that prevents Him. These three uses show that "deliver" can mean sometimes to submit, sometimes to gratify, sometimes to abandon to a fate.
H4042.portee: This word helps the believer grasp God's sovereignty over history and nations: He "delivers" victory or judgment according to His will and justice. But it also teaches that God can be in tension between justice and mercy: He "delivers" reluctantly, torn by love. It is a word that brings peace: God never delivers us without reason, and never without an internal debate with His love.

sens: Defensive weapon carried on the arm to protect against blows and projectiles
Divine protection against danger and evil
H4043.detail:
1. The shield is a defensive weapon that soldiers carried on their arm to cover themselves in battle. It was an essential piece of military equipment: Rehoboam had many made "of bronze" for his warriors (1 Kings 14:27), and the military leaders of Uzziah distributed them to his entire army along with spears and helmets (2 Chronicles 26:14). The shield protected the entire body of the one holding it.
2. In the language of faith, the shield becomes an image of divine protection. God Himself is compared to a shield for those who trust in Him: "I am your shield," says the Lord to Abram (Genesis 15:1), and the psalmist proclaims, "The Lord God is a sun and a shield" for those who walk in integrity (Psalms 84:12). The believer can also ask God to be his shield against his enemies: "Be my shield, be my strength" (Psalms 28:7). This protection is total: "He is a shield for all who trust in Him" (Psalms 18:31).
H4043.origine: The Hebrew word מָגֵן comes from a root meaning "to cover" or "to protect." The basic image is that of an object placed in front of oneself to take cover. The term evokes the idea of covering, of active defense. In biblical thought, moving from physical weaponry to divine protection was natural: just as the shield protects the soldier from the enemy's arrows, God protects the faithful from evil.
H4043.emploi: The word "shield" appears about 60 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical books and the Psalms. It first refers to concrete military equipment: the kings of Judah hoarded them in their arsenals (1 Kings 10:17, 2 Chronicles 9:16), and armies were equipped with them (2 Samuel 1:21, Jeremiah 46:3, Ezekiel 38:4). But the most important is its spiritual and poetic use: particularly in the Psalms and prophetic words, the shield becomes the classic image of God's protection over His people. The psalmists use it to express their trust: "Lord, you are my shield" (Psalms 3:4), "the Lord is my fortress and my shield" (Psalms 28:7). The meaning does not fundamentally change: it is always protection, but it moves from the military domain to the spiritual domain.
H4043.portee: For the believer, this word teaches that God is not distant, but active and present to defend him. The shield reminds us that divine protection is neither passive nor abstract: it covers the faithful just as a soldier covers himself with armor. This invites concrete trust, not fear, when facing trials. Finally, this image reminds us that our true security does not rest on our strength or weapons, but on our relationship with God.

sens: Obstruction, closing of the heart that prevents understanding or obedience
State of spiritual blindness or insensitivity to the truth
H4044.detail:
1. The word first designates a covering or veil that obstructs, that closes: like a membrane that covers the heart and isolates it. In Lamentations 3:65, this is what the prophet asks God: "You will deliver them to the hardening of their heart"—It is about allowing hearts to harden and close, incapable of feeling or understanding. It is a moral and spiritual numbness.
2. Hardening evokes the blindness of the heart: not ignorance, but the active refusal or acquired inability to see. It is when the inner being, instead of being open to God, progressively locks itself, as if covered by a thickening bark.
H4044.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to cover" or "to hide." To put a veil over something obscures it, isolates it from the rest. Applied to the heart, it evokes this progressive covering that makes it impermeable: this is what happens to those who refuse God's correction or grace, as described in the laments of the prophet Jeremiah.
H4044.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Lamentations 3:65. Jeremiah intercedes for his suffering people; in reviewing the causes of this suffering, he also states the judgment that falls on those who have rejected him. "The hardening of the heart" is then the divine punishment—not an external violence, but God's permission to allow the heart to progressively close in on itself, a natural and terrible consequence of the repeated refusal of His word.
H4044.portee: This word reminds us that the hardening of the heart is not an accident: it is a process that can reach us when we refuse to hear God. It invites us to pray to remain open to His voice and not to let our hearts become covered and engulfed in spiritual insensitivity.

sens: A stern word addressed to someone to blame or warn them
Reproach or reprimand that expresses discontent
Expression of divine reproach, sign of God's judgment
H4045.detail:
1. The word designates a harsh and severe word addressed to someone for reprimanding or correcting them — a form of blame that seeks to make reason understood. In Deuteronomy 28:20, it is a "threat" that God sends against Israel, in other words, a solemn warning accompanied by reproach, which manifests His discontent with their unfaithfulness.
2. It is a reproach or reprimand: the word expresses the critical judgment made on someone's reprehensible actions. The "threat" in this passage reveals that God sees and disapproves of the wickedness of Israel, who has abandoned Him.
3. On a spiritual level, this threat is a sign of divine judgment, accompanied by concrete misfortunes: it does not remain vain, but manifests itself through plagues and calamities. It is a fearsome word that brings trouble and destruction upon the unfaithful people.
H4045.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of shaking, agitating, or forcefully pushing away. The "threat" is therefore a word that stirs the soul, shaking it through reproach and warning. In the biblical context, it often expresses the Lord's reproach directed at His people: a word that shakes and warns.
H4045.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the context of the curses listed by Moses in Deuteronomy 28. It is found amidst a list of punishments — curse, trouble, destruction — that God will send to those who break the covenant. This "threat" is not a mere word, but a threatening reality that will materialize in the misfortunes and death promised to the unfaithful.
H4045.portee: This threat reminds the believer that God is not indifferent to unfaithfulness or wickedness: His word of reproach is fearsome and carries consequences. It invites one to take the covenant with the Lord seriously and not to abandon communion with Him for fear of attracting divine judgment.

sens: deadly blow or serious wound
military defeat, massacre in battle
epidemic disease or plague sent by God
divine judgment that strikes a people
sudden death of a large number of people
H4046.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a blow or wound that kills: a fatal blow inflicted on someone (1 Samuel 4:17 speaks of Israel's defeat against the Philistines as a "great plague").

2. In a military context, it refers to a bloody defeat, a massacre in battle where many fall (2 Samuel 17:9: "There is a plague among the people who follow Absalom").

3. The word also designates an epidemic disease, a pestilence: an affliction that spreads and kills quickly (Zechariah 14:12 describes a plague that consumes the flesh of the enemies of Jerusalem).

4. It is especially the punishment sent by God: the ten plagues of Egypt (Exodus 9:14), the plague that strikes Israel after sin (Numbers 16:49-50: the plague stops when Aaron intercedes), that of the census (2 Samuel 24:21).

5. The term can also refer to sudden and massive death, a divine strike that takes life (Numbers 25:8-9: Phinehas stops the plague by killing the sinners, but twenty-four thousand Israelites are already dead).
H4046.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to strike" or "to hit." It is related to other Hebrew terms designating a blow or an injury. The basic image is that of a violent blow delivered, from which the idea of injury, massacre, and then manifest and sudden divine punishment arises.
H4046.emploi: This word appears 25 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the context of divine judgment. The most memorable uses are the ten plagues of Egypt (Exodus 9:14 and other passages in Exodus), where God strikes the land to compel Pharaoh to let Israel go. It is also frequently found to describe the punishments that strike Israel itself after its revolts: the plague after idolatry (Numbers 25:8-9), that of the census of the people (2 Samuel 24:21; 1 Chronicles 21:17), that which follows the murmuring against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:48-50). David pleads with God that the plague does not strike his people (1 Chronicles 21:17). Phinehas stops a plague by his zeal (Psalms 106:30). The word designates both natural calamities (epidemics) and military defeats: both are seen as acts of God.
H4046.portee: This word reminds us that God is not indifferent to sin: He strikes to warn and to judge. The plagues demonstrate His power over nature and history, and His desire to bring His people back to obedience. They also teach that intercession (like that of Aaron or Phinehas) can stop judgment, and that the consequences of sin are real and sometimes collective. For the Christian, the plagues remind us of the seriousness of turning away from God and the importance of repentance.

sens: Leader of Israel at the time of Nehemiah who signed the covenant
H4047.detail: Magpiasch is a leader of the Jewish people, mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Israelites returned from exile renew their commitment to the covenant with God. He is among the official signatories of the covenant document drafted during Nehemiah's time (Nehemiah 10:20), alongside other leaders, such as Meshullam and Hezir. His name appears in a solemn list of the people's leaders who commit to observing the Law of Moses.
H4047.origine: The name Magpiasch means "mite killer" or "one who chases butterflies" (from the verb meaning to strike or kill and the noun designating a type of insect). It is a typical Hebrew name from the return from exile, a time when names often seem to describe traits or actions.
H4047.emploi: Magpiasch appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:20. He is named among the leaders of Judah who sign the covenant document after the return from exile in Babylon. This list marks a crucial moment in Israel's history: the solemn reaffirmation of the commitment to live according to the Law of Moses, after the reconstruction of the Temple and the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership. His inclusion in this official list indicates that he held some authority among the people.

sens: To project something forcefully downward or away from oneself
To deliver someone to danger or to an enemy
H4048.detail:
1. The word describes the action of projecting something forcefully, particularly downward. In Psalms 89:45, the psalmist says that God has "thrown" the king's throne to the ground: this is not to gently place it, but to violently overturn it, as one throws an object to destroy or humiliate it. It is an image of fall and disgrace.

2. The word can also mean "to deliver" someone to a dire fate, particularly to death or to the enemy. In Ezekiel 21:17, the princes of Israel are "delivered" to the sword: they are abandoned, left defenseless to death. The sense is less of a physical gesture than of a dark destiny from which one cannot escape.
H4048.origine: The Hebrew verb מָגַר (magar) expresses the idea of projecting, throwing with force. It is related to words that denote acts of violence or destruction. The related Aramaic מְגַר (megar) reinforces this notion by meaning "to overturn" or "to bring down." The word always evokes a brutal and irrevocable action, never a gentle or deliberate movement.
H4048.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 89:45, it describes the rejection of the royal throne: God "throws" to the ground the splendor and power of the king, an image of divine judgment and humiliation. In Ezekiel 21:17, it expresses the idea of delivering the princes to death by the sword, showing how God can abandon His people to invasion and massacre. In both cases, the word emphasizes a definitive and catastrophic action, with no possibility of return.
H4048.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment, when it comes, is irrevocable and total. There are no half-measures: a throne is not "thrown" halfway to the ground, and one does not "deliver" partially to the sword. For the reader, this invites a serious consideration of divine justice and an understanding that rebelling against God leads to inevitable downfall. It is also a call to repentance before this judgment arrives.

sens: To make something or someone fall from its established position
To destroy the order, plans of someone
H4049.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of making fall, to topple, to bring down what was standing or established. In Ezra 6:12, Darius prays that God will "overthrow" any king or people who would dare to threaten the house of the Lord: the image is that of a force that strikes down, that defeats an opponent or destroys them.
2. More broadly, to overthrow means to annul, destroy, or thwart someone's plans. It is the divine intervention that breaks, that annihilates the evil work of one who would oppose God's orders.
H4049.origine: This Aramaic word (méghar) is the causative form (Pael) of the verb מָגַר (magar), which literally means "to throw, to cast." The causative form intensifies the meaning: it means "to make throw," "to make fall" — hence "overthrow." It is a verb of direct and energetic action, where God intervenes to bring down what opposes Him.
H4049.emploi: The verb appears only once in the provided Aramaic New Testament, in Ezra 6:12. It is an edict from King Darius asking God to overthrow anyone attempting to transgress his orders regarding the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem. The usage is solemn and royal: this word expresses a curse, an invocation to divine power to annihilate the enemies of the temple and the order established by the authority of the king.
H4049.portee: This word reminds the reader that God does not abandon His people or His house. Even in the face of the powers of the world — here represented by kings and peoples — God intervenes to overthrow, to annihilate what opposes His word. For the Christian, this is a reason for confidence: no one can stand if they rise against the order and will of God.

sens: A toothed blade tool for cutting wood or stone
The action of sawing, cutting with this tool
H4050.detail:
1. The saw is a working instrument with a toothed blade, used to cut stone or wood along a line. In 1 Kings 7:9, the magnificent stones of the temple were cut "sawn with the saw, inside and outside": the saw allowed for precise and regular cuts according to measurements.
2. The word also refers to the action of sawing, cutting with the saw. In 2 Samuel 12:31 and 1 Chronicles 20:3, saws are listed among the instruments of torture used against the conquered inhabitants of the Ammonite cities: here, the word refers not only to the tool but to its brutal and deadly use.
H4050.origine: The Hebrew word מֶגֶרָה (mégérah) comes from a root meaning "to scrape" or "to scratch." The saw functions, in fact, as an instrument that "scrapes" the surface of the material in multiple successive strokes. The word belongs to the technical vocabulary of the wood and stone trades in the Old Testament.
H4050.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. Two occurrences (2 Samuel 12:31 and 1 Chronicles 20:3) describe the same event: David treats the Ammonite captives, and the saws are enumerated among other instruments of extreme punishment. A third occurrence (1 Kings 7:9) places the saw in a context of prestigious construction: the stones of Solomon's temple were carefully sawed to fit perfectly. The contrast is striking: in the first two texts, the saw is an instrument of torture; in the third, an instrument of craftsmanship and beauty.
H4050.portee: This word confronts us with the stark reality of violence in ancient Israel, including under David's reign, devoid of any idealism. But it also speaks to human labor and technical mastery: the builder's saw shapes the beauty of the temple, while the warrior's saw causes death. The word reminds us that the same tool can serve or destroy, depending on the hand that wields it and the intention of the heart.

sens: Place name or geographical formation near Gibeah and Michmash, in northern Israel
H4051.detail: Migron is a location situated near Gibeah, in the mountainous region of Benjamin, not far from Michmash. The name means "precipice" and likely evokes a characteristic rock formation or cliff of the terrain. In 1 Samuel 14:2, King Saul stands there with his troops during the campaign against the Philistines. In Isaiah 10:28, Migron appears as a waypoint on the route taken by an enemy army descending from the north towards Jerusalem. It is a geographical landmark that the listeners of the time would easily recognize.
H4051.origine: The Hebrew name מִגְרוֹן (Migron) comes from a root that evokes the idea of a precipice or steep slope. It designates a natural formation of the landscape, characteristic of the highlands of Benjamin where this place was located. Place names in ancient Israel often bore descriptive names related to their topography.
H4051.emploi: Migron appears only twice in the Bible. In 1 Samuel 14:2, it marks the place where Saul establishes his royal camp before an attack on a Philistine garrison, alongside a notable grenadier. In Isaiah 10:28, it is mentioned as a stop on the path that an enemy army (the Assyrians) takes as they descend to attack Jerusalem. In both cases, it is a territorial landmark to the north of the capital, important for military movements.

sens: Withdrawal or gradual decrease in width
Notch or setback in a construction
Space made between two surfaces
Ledge or edge serving as support
H4052.detail: 1. The word denotes a gradual decrease: each level of the temple was wider than the one below, creating successive recesses or setbacks. In 1 Kings 6:6, the three stories of the annexes of the temple increase progressively in width (5, then 6, then 7 cubits), meaning that at each level, a recess was made, that is, a sort of step or horizontal ledge that recessed inward. 2. It is an architectural notch: an area where the wall "recedes" to allow the upper floor to rest on the lower wall without the framework penetrating the thickness of the outer walls. 3. Concretely, it is a small space, a retreat of a few cubits, that helps the structure stand and gives the facade a stepped or terraced appearance.
H4052.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of decrease, reduction. The recess is literally an area where the plan reduces, where the surface diminishes. It is an image of withdrawal or stepping back in construction.
H4052.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 6:6, to describe the three stories of the chambers built around Solomon's temple. Each of these stories was designed with a recess so that the beams and framework could rest on these small ledges without damaging the main walls of the temple. It is therefore a technical term of sacred architecture, very precise, that shows the care taken in the construction of the temple.

sens: A piece of hardened earth with its roots and grass
An object thrown or cast by hand
Figuratively: a dry residue, a sterile remnant of what was rich
H4053.detail: 1. A clod is literally a piece of compact earth, lifted with its roots and grass, as obtained by digging or tilling the soil. It represents living, fertile soil that nourishes. 2. By extension, it refers to something that can be grasped and thrown, an object of the hand — which evokes the etymological link with the shovel or fork. 3. In Joel 1:17, the prophet uses this word to describe the horror of famine: the seeds are dried up, the granaries are empty, and only dead clods remain — the image of land emptied of its substance, where only the sterile crust remains. It is the antithesis of abundant harvest.
H4053.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the action of scraping, digging, or lifting the earth — which naturally produces these blocks of soil. The same family can be recognized in other Hebrew words related to working the land and the shovel. The initial image is that of the hand grasping and throwing, or of the soil being turned over.
H4053.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Joel 1:17. The prophet Joel denounces the catastrophic effects of a locust invasion: the crops are devoured, the land no longer produces, and all that remains for the farmers are dried clods — the very image of sterility and disaster. It is a highly concrete term, drawn from the vocabulary of the farmer.
H4053.portee: This word reminds us that fertility and abundance are gifts from God, not entitlements. When only the clod remains, it is a sign of judgment and the absence of blessing. For the reader, it embodies the threat of emptiness and desolation, and calls for recognition towards God for every harvest He grants.

sens: open land, cleared space around a city
common grazing area
common lands belonging to a community
space reserved for the collective use of a city or tribe
H4054.detail:
1. The word primarily designates open and cleared land surrounding a fortified city: it is the unbuilt space between the walls and the surrounding fields. In Joshua 21:13, it is stated that the city of Hebron and its "suburb" were given to the priests; this suburb was the immediately available space around the city.
2. This space served as pasture and communal land for livestock and agricultural activities of a city: the inhabitants grazed their herds there and harvested fodder. Numbers 35:3 and 35:4 precisely describe how these suburbs were reserved for the Levitical cities for livestock and cultivated fields.
3. For the cities of the Levites specifically, the suburb was a perpetual possession: it could not be sold, unlike the fields beyond (Leviticus 25:34). It was a guarantee of autonomy and sustenance for those who served in worship.
4. The word extends to any space reserved for the collective use of a city, whether intended for grazing, crops, or future urban expansions, as shown by the numerous occurrences in the distribution of cities to the Levites in Joshua 21 and 1 Chronicles 6.
H4054.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to expel" or "to reject" (hence "free, cleared space"). In Hebrew, the word was quite common to designate any open land belonging to a community. It is an administrative and legal term that expresses the idea of collective territory distinct from the city itself and the more distant private lands.
H4054.emploi: The word appears 69 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the context of land distribution to the Levites after the conquest of Canaan. It is heavily featured in Joshua 21 and 1 Chronicles 6, where each of the cities given to the Levites is mentioned with its respective suburb. The text of Numbers 35:2-5 establishes the legal framework: each Levitical city was to have a suburb of two thousand cubits in radius, designated for livestock and crops. In Leviticus 25:34, it is specified that these suburbs cannot be sold: they remain the perpetual property of the cities. Ezekiel uses it to describe the lands reserved for the future sanctuary and the holy city (45:2, 48:15-17).
H4054.portee: This word reminds us that God provided materially for those He consecrated to His service: the Levites did not have land inheritance like the other tribes, but cities with their suburbs to live and graze their animals. It is a lesson on God's care for His servants and on the just organization of a community: even in ancient Israel, there were common lands, spaces reserved for the use of all.

sens: A piece of fabric worn on the body
Cloth, textile
Rug or covering
Measure, dimension
H4055.detail:
1. The primary and most common meaning is a garment that one wears, a piece of clothing. It particularly refers to an outer garment, such as a tunic or robe. In Leviticus 6:3, the priest wears his linen tunic; in 1 Samuel 17:38-39, Saul dresses David in his own garments and armor.
2. The word can simply refer to fabric, cloth, the material from which garments are made. It is the idea of clothing reduced to its raw material.
3. By extension, it applies to textile objects other than the garments worn on oneself: in Judges 5:10, it speaks of rugs on which one sits, showing that the word covers any piece of fabric or linen.
4. In some passages, it can also refer to a measure or dimension, probably due to a semantic proximity with notions of content and proportion, although this meaning is less frequent in biblical Hebrew.
H4055.origine: The Hebrew word mad comes from a root that evokes the idea of measure, extent, and dimension. Hebrew words of the same family revolve around the notion of measuring, delimiting, evaluating the size or quantity of something. It is an ancient and common word in the Old Testament, used to designate what is measured and covered, hence its natural shift towards clothing: one measures a garment, one spreads it over the body. The notion of fabric or linen that can be spread out and measured has led to its widespread use for any textile object.
H4055.emploi: The word mad appears about 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, Judges) and the poetic books (Psalms, Job). Its primary usage is that of clothing in the literal and concrete sense: garments that one puts on, that are torn as a sign of mourning (1 Samuel 4:12), that are belted with a girdle (Judges 3:16). Sometimes, the text refers more to fabric or linen: in Judges 5:10, it explicitly concerns rugs. The word can also appear in metaphorical contexts: in Psalms 109:18 or Jeremiah 13:25, the garment sometimes symbolizes covering, protection, or what adheres to the skin. However, the word never takes on a marked spiritual charge; it is a term of everyday life.
H4055.portee: Understanding this term enriches our reading of the biblical narrative by recalling the details of clothing in ancient times. When David dons Saul's armor or when the priest wears his linen tunic, these verses show us a concrete, embodied piety: it is in the body and its adornments that religious function and obedience are lived out. Nudity or the tearing of garments expresses mourning or disgrace. This simple word grounds us in the material reality of the biblical world and helps us visualize the scenes we read.

sens: Stone or wooden structure intended for sacrifices and offerings
Place of meeting between God and His people
H4056.detail: 1. The altar is a structure, usually made of stone or wood, erected to offer sacrifices to God. It is a central liturgical piece of worship: animals are burned on it, and libations are poured. In Ezra 7:17, King Artaxerxes orders the purchase of bulls, rams, and lambs for "the offerings and the libations" on the altar of the temple in Jerusalem. 2. Beyond its material function, the altar symbolizes the point of contact between heaven and earth, where God accepts the offering of the people and responds to their prayers. It is a holy place, separated from the profane, where acts that restore or maintain the covenant with the God of Israel take place.
H4056.origine: The Aramaic word "madbach" is borrowed from the Hebrew "mizbeach" (מִזְבֵּחַ, H4196), which literally means "place of sacrifice" or "place where one slaughters." The Hebrew root evokes the act of sacrificing victims. The word appears in its Aramaic form in the passages of the Book of Ezra written in Aramaic, the administrative language of the Persian Empire. This form is therefore a cultural and linguistic "doublet" of the well-known Hebrew word.
H4056.emploi: The word appears only once in the entire Bible, in Ezra 7:17, in the Aramaic portion of the Book of Ezra. This passage recounts King Artaxerxes' decree allowing Ezra to send money to Jerusalem to restore the temple worship. Ezra must use this money to buy the animals necessary for sacrifices and libations on the altar of the temple. Although it appears only once, this word refers to the same cultic reality as its Hebrew equivalent "mizbeach," which is omnipresent in the Old Testament.
H4056.portee: This word reminds the reader that the temple worship, far from being a mere habit or local practice, was supported by the political authorities themselves. God used pagan kings to ensure the maintenance of worship and sacrifices. It is a testimony to divine sovereignty: even in exile or under foreign domination, God preserves the means of access to Him through sacrifice and offering.

sens: The opening of the face through which one breathes, eats, and speaks
The organ of speech and expression
What the mouth expresses or reveals about the heart and soul
H4057A.detail:
1. The mouth is primarily the physical opening of the face, the place of vital breath and food. It is the instrument by which one communicates with others.
2. Used for speaking, the mouth becomes the organ of speech: it expresses the thoughts, will, and feelings of the one who possesses it. What one says reveals who one truly is.
3. From a more spiritual and moral perspective, the mouth symbolizes everything that emanates from a person — their words, promises, and intentions. In Song of Solomon 4:3, "your mouth is lovely" evokes not only physical beauty but also the sweetness of the one expressing: her mouth fascinates with its grace and charm.
H4057A.origine: The Hebrew word מִדְבָּר (midbar) comes from a root that literally designates the speaking opening, that which opens to produce speech and breath. Its primitive etymology refers to the act of speaking or pronouncing. The term applies to the mouth as a living instrument, the seat of human communication.
H4057A.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided biblical text, in Song of Solomon 4:3, where the lover celebrates the beauty of the one he loves. Her "mouth is lovely": this is a compliment that unites physical beauty and the expressiveness of the person. In the context of the Song, the mouth is one of the parts of the face listed to praise the beloved, revealing both her material beauty and the charm of what she expresses.
H4057A.portee: For the Christian reader, the mouth reminds us of the importance of monitoring our words and allowing our regenerated hearts to express themselves. It also symbolizes the grace of being able to speak to God in prayer, to confess our faith, and to share the Gospel. The beauty and purity of what comes out of our mouths reflect what we have become in Christ.

sens: Arid and uninhabited land, lacking water and vegetation
Grazing or transit area
Wild region far from cities
Spiritual trial or solitude
H4057B.detail:
1. The desert is primarily an arid, dry region with no permanent inhabitants — it is the rocky or sandy terrain where water is scarce. Thus, the desert of Maon or that of Moab refer to real expanses that the Israelites traverse (1 Samuel 23:24 and Deuteronomy 2:8).

2. It is also an area where flocks graze and where one can take refuge or camp: Moses asks the Midianite to stay with Israel as a guide "in the desert" where they camp (Numbers 10:31), for although it is a desert, it is a space for nomadic life.

3. The desert can designate a traversed region, a transit area: the Israelites travel through it, passing through (Jeremiah 9:10: "on the plains of the desert I utter a lament"), far from urban civilization.

4. On a spiritual level, the desert embodies trial, deprivation, and testing of faith: Psalm 78:19 recalls Israel's hunger when they say, "Can God prepare a table in the desert?", revealing doubt in the absence.
H4057B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to graze" or "to be empty, bare." It first designates a grazing area or a transit land, then applies to the vast desert expanses of the Near East. In Hebrew, the word initially carried the idea of an open and exposed place, accessible to flocks but inhospitable. This is why the same notion expresses both grazing (a place where one can live) and the radical desert (where life dies).
H4057B.emploi: The word appears more than 250 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Exodus, Numbers, and Psalms. It is a key term in the history of Israel: the desert of Sinai is the central place of the covenant and the giving of the Law (Exodus 19:1), but also of the 40 years of wandering (Numbers 14:32-33). David takes refuge there fleeing from Saul (1 Samuel 23:24). Jeremiah paints it as a space of moral desolation (Jeremiah 9:10). The desert represents both a place of trials and encounters with God, a space of purification and revelation.
H4057B.portee: The desert in the Bible is never neutral: it is where God educates His people, tests them, and miraculously nourishes them, where He reveals Himself. For the Christian, the desert invites meditation on faith in adversity, trust in God when everything seems lacking, and the path of spiritual purification. It is also a reminder that God walks with His own even in isolation and trial.

sens: Arid region devoid of trees, populated by rare life
Bare space that tests and isolates the one who traverses it
Territory where God leads His people to the school of faith
H4057G.detail:
1. The desert is primarily a geographical region: arid lands, without abundant water or vegetation, where living is difficult. It is the landscape of Sinai, where Moses received the Law of the Lord (Leviticus 7:38).
2. It is also a place of solitude and trial, where one faces their needs and God. Those who enter the desert must rely on divine help, not on their own resources.
3. Spiritually, the desert becomes the school of faith: God leads His people there to purify, instruct, and draw them closer to Him. It is in the desert that a new generation capable of entering the Promised Land is born.
H4057G.origine: The Hebrew word midbar comes from a root meaning "to lead to pasture" or "to speak," as if the desert were the place where God "speaks" to His people. The desert of Sinai is not just an obstacle: it is a space of encounter with the Lord, where He reveals His will and covenant.
H4057G.emploi: This word appears once in the provided usages, but it is in a crucial context: Leviticus 7:38 mentions the desert of Sinai as the place where the Lord prescribed to Moses the worship and offerings. It is in the desert that God gives the structure of Israel's worship. The desert is thus presented not merely as a landscape, but as the place of transmission of divine will and establishment of the covenant.
H4057G.portee: For the Christian, the desert reminds us that God uses trials and solitude to form faith. The "desert" moments of life are not absences of God: it is often there that He speaks most clearly and renews His covenant with us. Trust in His provision replaces earthly comfort.

sens: Determine the dimensions or length of something using an instrument or a reference unit
Evaluate a quantity by comparing it to a standard measure
Traverse a distance by measuring it
Extend, occupy a certain spatial extent
Assess, appreciate the value or importance of something
H4058.detail:
1. To measure is to precisely determine the dimensions of an object or a structure with an instrument (a cord, a rod, an omer). Ezekiel 40:9 clearly shows this: the angel measures the entrance hall of the gate and finds eight cubits deep and two cubits for the posts.
2. Measuring a quantity means checking its conformity to an established measure: in Exodus 16:18, the Israelites measure the manna with the omer so that each receives their fair share, neither more nor less.
3. Measuring a distance means traversing the terrain while evaluating its dimensions: in 2 Samuel 8:2, David measures the defeated Moabites by making them lie down, thus determining how many he would keep or eliminate.
4. The word can mean "to extend" or "to cover" an area: Psalms 108:8 speaks of God measuring the valley of Succoth, meaning He takes possession of it by establishing its boundaries.
5. Figuratively, to measure means to evaluate or appreciate: the context of Job 7:4 suggests measuring the hours of the night, meaning to count and assess them.
H4058.origine: The root madad expresses the fundamental idea of extending, deploying: from which derive "measure" (middah) and "extent." The verb has several forms: the simple form (Qal) means to measure a given reality; the intensive or repeated form (Piel) adds the idea of prolonging, continuing; the reflexive form (Hithpolel) describes one who extends themselves. The basic image is that of the gesture of one who unfolds a cord or a ruler to grasp a length.
H4058.emploi: Madad appears 49 times in the Old Testament, often in technical and architectural contexts, particularly in the detailed vision of the temple given to Ezekiel (chapters 40 to 47): the angel guiding Ezekiel measures each part of the buildings and their courtyards. It is also found in practical uses: measuring the manna (Exodus 16:18), distributing the spoils (2 Samuel 8:2), determining the city of refuge (Numbers 35:5). Three passages (Psalms 60:8 and 108:8, Hosea 2:1) use the verb in the figurative sense of "to share" or "to delimit," as if God were tracing the borders of the territory by measuring it. No major nuance changes the fundamental meaning: it is always the act of precisely determining a dimension or an extent.
H4058.portee: For the Christian reader, this word emphasizes God's precision and order. In Ezekiel's vision of the temple, each measurement reveals a God who knows exactly the proportions of His sanctuary: nothing is left to chance. In Psalms 108:8, God "measures" His territory, thus affirming His absolute sovereignty. The word invites recognition that God masters all realities, great and small, and that He establishes boundaries with perfect wisdom. It is also an implicit invitation to accept the measures and limits that God sets for our lives.

sens: The act of measuring something, or the result of this measurement: its dimension, its size
The dimension or extent of a thing, its format or size
A portion of space or matter that is delimited and determined
A unit or instrument used for measuring
The size or stature of a person
H4060A.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the act of measuring or the immediate result of that act. It is to compare something to a standard to know its size. For example, in Exodus 26:2, the tapestries of the sanctuary have a common "measure": each has been measured and all are twenty-eight cubits long. 2. It then refers to the dimension or format of a thing considered in itself. In 1 Kings 7:9, the stones of the temple are "cut according to measures": each has a determined size to fit its place in the construction. 3. The word can also mean a portion or a section that is delimited: in Nehemiah 3:20, each worker "repairs a portion" of the wall, meaning a defined length section. 4. Sometimes it designates the measuring instrument itself: in Ezekiel 42:16, the "rod that served as a measure" is the tool with which the dimensions of the temple are measured. 5. Finally, applied to a person, it expresses size or stature: in Isaiah 45:14, the Ethiopians are men "of tall stature."
H4060A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to measure" or "to extend." It is a noun formed on the idea of establishing a precise dimension, a limit. The family of the word includes verbs and nouns related to the action of delimiting, defining the extent of a thing. The basic image is that of a cord or instrument that marks the boundaries of a space.
H4060A.emploi: The word appears 51 times, mainly in the architectural and technical descriptions of the Hebrew Bible. It is very frequent in the description of Solomon's temple and the future temple seen by Ezekiel, where each dimension is given with precision. It is also found in Nehemiah to describe the portions of wall that each worker repairs. In Leviticus 19:35 and Numbers 13:32, it refers to a just or exact measure. The word can designate the act of measuring (an action), the size of a thing or a person, a delimited portion, or the measuring instrument itself. Its meaning refines according to the context: architectural, constructive, or physical when it concerns stature.
H4060A.portee: This word speaks of the order and precision that God brings to His creation and His plan. The temple, measured exactly in every detail, shows that God is not a God of disorder, but of wisdom and harmony. For the believer, this invites trust: God "measures" our life and His conduct is exact and just. It also calls us to honesty and integrity: to use just measures in our dealings, as the Law teaches.

sens: tax or fee to be paid to the king or ruling authority
forced contribution levied on a subjugated people
H4060B.detail:
1. Tribute is a sum of money imposed by royal authority on the lands, harvests, or income of subjects. In Nehemiah 5:4, the Jews who were rebuilding Jerusalem had to borrow money to pay the tribute to the king of Persia: it is a mandatory financial burden, not voluntary, weighing heavily on the inhabitants.
2. More broadly, it is the concrete expression of a people's submission to a foreign or dominant power — a form of regular ransom that politically manifests dependence and subjugation.
H4060B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root denoting the idea of measure or assigned portion — tribute being literally the portion that is "measured" and collected mandatorily. In Aramaic (the language spoken in Persia), the word takes the form *mindah* and also refers to the tax collected by royal administration. This vocabulary is rooted in the administrative reality of ancient empires, where tribute was a major instrument of fiscal domination.
H4060B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible translated by Segond, in Nehemiah 5:4. This historical context shows the Jews under Persian domination in the 5th century B.C., forced to pay taxes to the king while undertaking reconstruction work. It is an administrative and political term that reflects the concrete condition of the people in exile: even returned from captivity, Jerusalem remains subject to a heavy tribute that impoverishes its inhabitants.
H4060B.portee: This word reminds us that the people of God have experienced periods of fiscal oppression and political servitude — a reality that reinforces trust in the liberation that only God can bring. It also invites vigilance: how do we live under present authorities, and how does God call us to respond to unjust demands while keeping the faith?

sens: Giant warrior from the time of the united monarchy, a member of the family of Rapha
H4060G.detail: Midden is a giant warrior mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time when David ruled over Israel. He belongs to the family of the Rephaim, formidable giants, and he is the brother of Goliath, the famous giant defeated by David. Like his brothers Ishbi-Benob, Saph, and Lahmi, Midden represents those exceptionally sized adversaries that the warriors of Israel had to face.
H4060G.origine: The name Midden means "of great size" or "man of great stature" in Hebrew. He belongs to the genealogy of the Rephaim, a lineage of giants, the most well-known of whom is Goliath. The biblical context places these giant warriors during the time of David and afterward, as descendants of Rapha, the eponymous ancestor of all these giants.
H4060G.emploi: Midden is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 20:6, where he is identified as a brother of Goliath and a member of the Rephaim clan. The passage presents him in the context of David's wars against enemy peoples. His unique appearance in the biblical text confirms that he participated in the conflicts of the time of the united monarchy, alongside giants who threatened the safety of Israel.

sens: Tax or levy imposed by a king or state on a conquered territory or population
Financial contribution imposed on a subjugated or vassal people
Revenue that the central authority derives from a region or province
H4061.detail:
1. The tribute is a tax that kings impose on the peoples they dominate or have conquered, in recognition of their power. In Ezra 4:20, it speaks of the powerful kings of Jerusalem "to whom tribute, tax, and toll were paid" — it is a financial burden that the population must fulfill.
2. The term also refers to the revenues that the king derives from a subjugated region, notably the goods and resources he can use for his projects. Ezra 6:8 specifies that the costs of rebuilding the temple will be "taken from the king's goods from the tributes on the other side of the river."
3. It is a burden that can be levied or exempted at the will of the sovereign. Ezra 7:24 lists the categories of people (priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers) from whom "neither tribute, nor tax, nor toll can be levied" — a royal exemption from these obligations.
H4061.origine: The Aramaic word *middah* (from the same root as the Hebrew *middah* in H4060B) comes from a root that originally denotes "measure" or "portion." From there, it took on the meaning of "assigned part" or "imposed contribution" — the tribute is a regular portion that each subject must pay to the royal treasury. This political and fiscal meaning is specific to the context of the Persian and Babylonian empires of the post-exilic period.
H4061.emploi: The word *middah* (Aramaic) appears 4 times in the book of Ezra, notably in the royal letters and decrees of the Persian kings Darius and Artaxerxes. It contrasts with other forms of revenue or burdens: "tribute, tax, and toll" (Ezra 4:20). The usages show that the tribute can be either a heavy burden on the territory or a resource that the king reallocates to projects of his choice, such as the rebuilding of the temple. The term reflects the tax administration of the Persian empire, at a time when Judea was a tributary province.
H4061.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the kings of this world exercise temporal power over territory and resources. It also illustrates how, even in exile and under foreign domination, God can transform human institutions to serve His plans: the tribute imposed by the Persian king becomes the means to finance the rebuilding of the temple. It is a reminder of divine providence acting within the workings of political power.

sens: Noisy and violent behavior, outburst of rage
Arrogant and haughty behavior
Tumult and agitation
H4062.detail:
1. The word denotes behavior that erupts in noise and violence, without restraint: someone who gives in to fits of anger or screams. In Isaiah 14:4, it describes the despot who oppressed the peoples through his rage and domineering arrogance.
2. It is also the insolence of one who believes himself above all, who despises and belittles others through his pride: the noisy arrogance of one who abuses his power.
3. The general image is that of agitation, tumult, and unmeasured fury expressed through harsh words and acts of domination.
H4062.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes noise, turbulence, and outburst. It belongs to a family of terms that describe behaviors marked by excess, lack of self-control, and brutal arrogance. The root emphasizes the idea of something that overflows, that does not hold back.
H4062.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 14:4, where the prophet pronounces a mocking song against the king of Babylon: "You will say this song about the king of Babylon… Behold, the insolence of the tyrant is over!" The context shows that this despot exercised his power with fury and violence, striking the peoples mercilessly. The term paints the arrogant fury of an oppressor whom God will bring down.
H4062.portee: This word reminds us that God sees and hates the brutal arrogance of those who dominate through violence and contempt. Isaiah's song announces that even the most powerful tyrant, whose insolence seems inevitable, will fall under the hand of God. It is a comfort for the oppressed and a warning for the proud.

sens: Clothing worn on the body
H4063.detail: 1. A garment, a piece of fabric that one wears to cover the body. In the two passages where this word appears, it refers to the tunics or robes worn by the servants of King David: Hanun orders them to be torn to the thighs to publicly humiliate them (2 Samuel 10:4).
H4063.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of covering or clothing. It belongs to the family of words that designate what envelops and protects the body. It is a simple and common term for everyday clothing, without particular connotation.
H4063.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, in two parallel accounts that relate the same event: the public humiliation of David's servants by King Hanun. In these two verses (2 Samuel 10:4 and 1 Chronicles 19:4), the garment is torn as an act of offense and contempt towards King David. The usage underscores the vulnerability of the human body and the intention of humiliation behind this act of violence against clothing.
H4063.portee: This passage reminds us that mistreating the servants of a king is a serious insult, worthy of retaliation. It also shows how clothing, a simple ordinary covering, becomes the instrument of public shame: forced nudity was considered one of the worst humiliations in biblical culture.

sens: condition that weakens or destroys the health of the body
affliction sent by God as punishment or trial
H4064.detail:
1. A disease is a condition that affects the body and makes it ill: it is the state of one who does not enjoy health. In Deuteronomy 7:15, the Lord promises to remove from His people all disease, particularly the evil diseases of Egypt that the Israelites know well.
2. In the Bible, diseases are often seen as plagues sent by God as a sign of judgment or punishment. In Deuteronomy 28:60, God threatens to bring upon disobedient Israel all the diseases of Egypt as a consequence of breaking the covenant: disease then becomes a formidable weapon of divine judgment.
H4064.origine: The Hebrew word madweh comes from a root that evokes the idea of being weak or downcast. It belongs to the family of terms that describe physical suffering and infirmity. This word emphasizes the debilitating aspect of disease: it weakens, it takes away strength.
H4064.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy. In Deuteronomy 7:15, it refers to the diseases from which God wants to protect His people — a promise of healing and preservation. In Deuteronomy 28:60, in the context of curses related to disobedience, the same diseases become a threat: they will cling to the one who breaks the covenant. The contrast shows that health is a blessing and disease a consequence of divine judgment.
H4064.portee: This disease reminds the reader that health is not taken for granted: it is a gift from God linked to obedience. For the Christian, this invites recognition that God is sovereign over life and death, strength and weakness, and that He can both test and deliver. It is also an invitation to seek first the kingdom and its righteousness, knowing that God's blessings include the well-being of the body.

sens: That which deceives, misleads
That which seduces away from the right path
False word or prophecy
H4065.detail:
1. The word designates that which deceives or misleads — a false promise, a lie, something that leads someone astray by causing them to deviate from their path. In Lamentations 2:14, the prophets give Jerusalem "deceptive oracles": instead of warning her of her sin so she can escape punishment, they tell her false stories that keep her in illusion and error.
2. It is something that seduces and leads astray — the image is one of seduction that diverts someone from their path. False prophets act as seducers: they attract the people by telling them what they want to hear, not what is true.
3. The word particularly applies to false words, to false prophecy that deceives the people about their spiritual condition and leaves them without hope of salvation, delivered to captivity.
H4065.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to remove, to distance, to divert." A deceiver is literally something that leads someone away from the truth, that pulls them aside. It is something that seduces and draws back — hence its meaning of seduction, enticement, something that diverts.
H4065.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 2:14. It is used to describe the false prophecies that the prophets gave to Jerusalem before its fall. It is a context of judgment and ruin: the false prophets, instead of warning the people of their sin, give them "deceptive oracles" that keep them in error and misdirection, preventing them from repenting and escaping catastrophe.
H4065.portee: This word reminds of the spiritual danger of false prophecies and deceptive words. It shows that failing to speak the truth in a timely manner contributes to the ruin of those to whom one lies. For the Christian, this warns against those who preach a smoothed-over, reassuring, and false gospel, and invites the search for the truth that sets free, even if it is disturbing.

sens: Dispute, conflict between two people or groups
Cause, motive, reason for disagreement
Trouble, agitation in a community
H4066.detail:
1. A quarrel is a dispute, a verbal confrontation or tension between people. The word evokes friction, the disagreement that arises — it is what happens when "a violent man stirs up quarrels" (Proverbs 15:18), creating repeated clashes.
2. The word also designates the issue of the conflict, that which the disagreement is about — "an object of discord" (Psalms 80:7): the quarrels that divide friends are often provoked by one who reports words (Proverbs 16:28).
3. The quarrel is a trouble that spreads within the community: it ignites and is maintained like a fire that needs fuel to burn (Proverbs 26:20), but it "is calmed" as soon as one stops feeding it. It is a movement of social friction that can degenerate if left to grow.
H4066.origine: The Hebrew word מָדוֹן comes from a root that expresses the idea of contention and struggle. The family of the word includes the idea of tension and conflict. In a biblical context, it is the common term to describe disputes and disagreements between humans — not physical violence (which would have another word), but relational and verbal conflict.
H4066.emploi: This word appears 10 times in the Old Testament, especially in Proverbs and in prophetic laments. It describes the ordinary quarrels that arise from difficult characters: the violent man (Proverbs 15:18), the perverse man who reports words (Proverbs 16:28), the one who loves to quarrel (Proverbs 29:22). It is also a sign of curse or social trouble: Israel is inflicted with quarrels with its neighbors (Psalms 80:7), and the prophets denounce quarrels as urban plagues (Habakkuk 1:3). The word remains constant: it is always about relational conflicts, never wars.
H4066.portee: Understanding that the quarrel has a human source — often pride, verbal violence, or gossip — helps the believer assess its seriousness and seek peace. Proverbs invite not to feed it, to let it die for lack of fuel (gossip, wounded pride). Recognizing that "starting a quarrel is like opening a dam" (Proverbs 17:14) invites preventive wisdom: it is better to withdraw before the harm amplifies. It is a call to moderation and the pursuit of reconciliation.

sens: Total height of a person's entire body
Stature or physical span considered as a sign of strength or greatness
H4067.detail:
1. Height is the total height of the body, measured from the foot to the top of the head — what one sees at a glance when encountering someone. In 2 Samuel 21:20, the giant from Gath stands out for his tall height, reminding that he descends from the race of the Rephaim, a lineage of fearsome giants.
2. Height can also evoke stature in the sense of impressive physical power: it is the span of a man considered as a whole, which makes him imposing or threatening. Here, the giant's great height underscores his superhuman and dangerous nature.
H4067.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that designates the length or dimension of an object or person. It belongs to the family of words describing measurements and proportions of the body. This concrete and observable term has no connection to abstract concepts: it simply paints what is seen.
H4067.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 21:20. It serves to characterize a giant, a member of the family of the Rephaim, born in Gath during a battle in David's time. The mention of his tall height prepares the reader to discover his other extraordinary traits: six fingers on each hand and foot. In this warrior context, excessive height signals a superhuman enemy, a danger that only David's warriors can defeat.
H4067.portee: This word reminds that in the biblical narrative, physical difference — exceptional height — can symbolize strangeness, power, or even threat. David and his men are not intimidated by giants: this passage invites the reader not to fear visible obstacles, however impressive they may be, when God is on our side.

sens: Canaanite city in the northern part of the land
H4068.detail: 1. Madon is a city located in Canaan, in the northern region, which was among the important and fortified cities of the land before the Israelite conquest. It is mentioned as one of the royal cities governed by its own king (Joshua 12:19).
H4068.origine: The name literally means "quarrel" or "strife" in Hebrew, but it refers here to a specific city in Canaan. The meaning of the name may evoke the conflicts that characterized the region at that time.
H4068.emploi: Madon appears twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Joshua, during the conquest of Canaan. It is first mentioned in Joshua 11:1 as one of the cities whose king received a message from Jabin, king of Hazor, calling him to form a coalition against Joshua and the Israelites. This coalition gathered at the waters of Merom for battle. Then, in Joshua 12:19, Madon is listed among the kings defeated by Joshua, confirming that its rebellion against Israel was crushed during this military campaign.

sens: direct inquiry about the cause or reason for an action
indirect or rhetorical inquiry expressing astonishment or protest
request for justification or reproach regarding behavior
question posed to God about the meaning of misfortunes or injustices
H4069.detail:
1. The word simply asks for the reason or cause of an action: "Why have you come to me, since you hate me?" (Genesis 26:27). This is the most direct and neutral question.
2. It expresses astonishment or concern in the face of something unexpected: Sisera's mother cries, "Why is his chariot so late in coming?" (Judges 5:28), anxious about his absence. Here, the word carries an emotion.
3. It is also a challenge or reproach: "Why then have you not kept the oath?" (1 Kings 2:43). The speaker contests and demands accountability.
4. In the wisdom literature and the prophets, the word becomes a question directed to God about the reason for suffering: "Why did I not find knees to receive me?" (Job 3:12), with Job wondering why he was born to suffer. It is an existential protest.
H4069.origine: The Hebrew word מַדּוּעַ (maddûa') comes from the root דוע, which means "to know" or "to understand." Its primary meaning is "what do we know?" that is, "what is the reason?" It is an inquiry seeking to know, to understand the hidden motive. The word is formed as a question that seeks this knowledge.
H4069.emploi: Used 71 times in the Old Testament, this word is a fundamental inquiry in the biblical narrative. In the historical accounts (Genesis, Samuel, Kings), it appears in dialogues: one character asks another to explain their action. In the Law (Exodus, Leviticus), it poses questions about divine ordinances. But it is especially in Job and Jeremiah that it takes on its prophetic and existential force: the believer questions God about the meaning of suffering and injustice. The prophet Jeremiah uses it to express Israel's protest against God: "Why has this people of Jerusalem turned away in perpetual backsliding?" (Jeremiah 8:5). It is a question that runs throughout Scripture, from the everyday to the theological.
H4069.portee: This word invites the believer not to passively accept what they do not understand. The Bible encourages asking questions, even difficult ones and even to God, as long as it is done sincerely. It shows that faith is not the absence of questions, but trust in asking those questions. Job can cry "Why?" because he knows that God listens to him. This word reminds us that the believer's life includes moments of seeking to understand the meaning of what happens to them.

sens: place where one lives, location where someone resides
condition of life, state in which one lives
H4070A.detail:
1. The word designates the place where one dwells, the location where someone has their home. It is a physical, concrete space: in Daniel 4:25, King Nebuchadnezzar is warned that he will "have his dwelling with the beasts of the field," meaning he will be reduced to living among wild animals, far from royal palaces.
2. More broadly, it also refers to the condition of life, the state in which one resides. The word evokes not only the place but the existential situation: living as a beast, sleeping outside, eating grass — all that accompanies this miserable "dwelling." In Daniel 5:21, we find this same image: the "dwelling" of the king who became mad is that of wild donkeys, summarizing his total humiliation and change of fate.
H4070A.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew מָגוֹר (magour), which means "dwelling," "temporary residence," "exile." The root fundamentally speaks of the act of inhabiting a place, of residing there. The word thus evokes a "place where one lies down," hence the image of a bed, a dwelling. It is a word from the family of terms that express habitation and lodging, but with a nuance of stay, sometimes unstable or imposed.
H4070A.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all three cases in the book of Daniel, in chapters 4 and 5. It always refers to the same episode: the punishment of King Nebuchadnezzar. In Daniel 4:25 and 4:32, the judgment that will strike him is stated: he will have his dwelling with the beasts. In Daniel 5:21, the fulfillment of the judgment is reported with his successor Belshazzar: his dwelling indeed became that of wild donkeys. The word carries a dramatic charge: it is the complete inversion of royal condition, the transition from palace to savagery. Each usage emphasizes the king's humiliation before the supreme God.
H4070A.portee: This word reminds us that dwelling and status are never definitive in the eyes of God. The Bible shows that even a powerful king can have his dignity stripped away and live like a beast if he refuses to acknowledge the Most High. It is a lesson in wisdom: true power belongs to God alone, and human pride can be humbled. For the believer, this invites humility and submission to the Creator rather than trusting in one's own power or wealth.

sens: Habitation, place where one resides
Residence, stay of a being or a power
H4070B.detail:
1. The word designates the place where someone or something lives: the house, the lodging where one stays. In Daniel 2:11, "the dwelling of the gods" means heaven, the celestial place where pagan deities reside — something inaccessible to humans, unlike a terrestrial dwelling.
2. More broadly, it is the stay, the living space proper to a being. The word emphasizes that everyone has their place, their spot where they dwell: the gods in heaven, humans on earth.
H4070B.origine: The Aramaic word מְדָר (medar) comes from the same root as the Hebrew מָגוֹר (magur, "dwelling," "residence"), the latter being formed from the root גור (gur) meaning "to stay" or "to dwell." These words express the idea of remaining in a place, of taking up residence there. Aramaic and Hebrew share this family of words to speak of lodging and dwelling.
H4070B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:11. In this context, Nebuchadnezzar reproaches the Babylonian magicians for being unable to interpret his dream, stating that only the gods could do so — and that "their dwelling is not among men." The word expresses here a radical separation: the gods live elsewhere, in an inaccessible world, while humans are on earth. It is an argument to show the human impossibility of the task.
H4070B.portee: This word reminds us that everyone has their assigned place: earthly creatures here below, and God in heaven. It highlights the infinite gap between the divine and the human — a truth that the wise of the world cannot overcome on their own. For the Christian reader, it raises the question of what remains with us: it is by grace that God, though celestial, draws near and dwells with His people.

sens: Stack of wood piled up to be set on fire
Elevated structure of wood or fuel for a sacrifice or punishment
H4071.detail:
1. The burnt offering is primarily a stack of wood piled up and prepared to be burned. In Isaiah 30:33, there is mention of a "deep" and "vast" burnt offering, where fire and wood abound, ready to be ignited by the breath of the Lord: it is an image of massive and inevitable divine judgment.
2. By extension, it is the structure on which something or someone is burned — whether it be a sacrifice or an execution. In Ezekiel 24:9, the Lord says He wants to make "a great burnt offering," a threatening image of the judgment that will fall upon Jerusalem for its iniquity.
H4071.origine: The Hebrew word מְדוּרָה comes from a root meaning "to dwell" or "to attach" (דּוּר), as a burnt offering is a pile where the wood is stacked and remains united. This same word describes swelling or accumulation, the idea of something that piles up and takes shape. The notion of the fire's "dwelling" is never far: the burnt offering is the hearth, the place where the fire "lives."
H4071.emploi: The word מְדוּרָה appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, solely in the prophets Isaiah and Ezekiel. In Isaiah 30:33, it refers to the burnt offering of divine judgment on Assyria, long prepared; in Ezekiel 24:9, it is that destined for Jerusalem. In both cases, the burnt offering symbolizes the fire of God's judgment, inevitable and terrible. The word never appears to designate the burnt offerings of Israelite worship: it is reserved for eschatological judgment.
H4071.portee: The burnt offering reminds us that God's judgment is not improvised or sudden: it is "long prepared." This image invites the reader to take the prophetic warning and the reality of judgment seriously. It also shows us that iniquity accumulates the fuel for judgment, as if each sin adds wood to the burnt offering. It is an invitation to repentance before the fire is lit.

sens: Destruction, collapse, annihilation
That which causes the fall or collapse of someone
H4072.detail:
1. Destruction, collapse, annihilation: the word designates the state of that which is crumbling, disintegrating, disappearing. It is the concrete image of a house crashing to the ground or a city razed. In Proverbs 26:28, the flattering mouth "prepares ruin": it sets in motion the conditions that destroy the one who listens, just as an earthquake destroys a building.
2. That which causes the fall or collapse of someone: the word can also refer to that which brings about destruction — the occasion to fall, the trap set, the false counsel that leads to annihilation. The flattering words of the verse thus become a living ruin, a mechanism of destruction.
H4072.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of fall, collapse. It belongs to the family of words that describe destruction and overturning — that which falls, that which no longer stands. Its primary meaning is very concrete: the landslide, the rubble, that which exists only in a state of ruins.
H4072.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 26:28. It describes the destructive effect of flattering words: the mouth that lies and flatters builds nothing; it produces only ruins. The wise man wants to warn his reader that beautiful deceitful words are a deadly trap, a mechanism that transforms the one who believes them into a destroyed person.
H4072.portee: This passage reminds the believer of the devastating power of flattering and deceitful words. We live in a world that coddles us, flatters us, tells us what we want to hear — often serving the lie. The Bible invites us to flee these words as one flees a collapsing house. Only the true word builds; flattering words build only ruins.

sens: action of causing someone to fall by pushing them
ruin or destruction that follows
action of chasing or expelling
disaster that strikes one who commits violence
H4073.detail: 1. The word first evokes the physical action of violently pushing someone, throwing them to the ground or making them topple. It is the gesture of the warrior who repels his opponent. 2. It then designates the resulting state: the ruin or fall of the one who has been overturned. In Psalms 140:12, the violent man "leads him to his loss" — he is heading for his own destruction. 3. The word can also evoke an expulsion, the action of driving someone far from their place. 4. Figuratively, it is the disaster that awaits one who sows violence: the Word affirms that the violent man does not stand firm but runs toward his loss, struck by the misfortune he has sown.
H4073.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the sudden movement of pushing away, throwing out. It belongs to the family of violent action verbs: to push, to chase, to precipitate. The image is that of physical shock and the collapse that follows.
H4073.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 140:12. It is found in a psalm of supplication where the poet asks God to protect him from those who plot evil. The context contrasts the man whose tongue is false and the violent man: both "do not stand firm on the earth," but the violent one runs to his own loss. The word expresses here divine judgment: he who sows violence reaps ruin.
H4073.portee: This verse teaches the Christian a profound truth: violence and lies never prosper. God does not abandon those who suffer it and ensures that injustice turns against the one who commits it. The reader finds both comfort and a warning: to place their trust in God rather than fear the persecutors.

sens: Son of Japheth, ancestor of an ancient people
The people of the Medes, descendants of this son of Japheth
The region inhabited by the Medes, in Western Asia
H4074G.detail:
