1. Madai is a man living in the time of the patriarchs, listed among the sons of Japheth alongside Gomer, Magog, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras (Genesis 10:2, 1 Chronicles 1:5). He represents the founding father of a lineage.
2. The people of the Medes descend from Madai: it is an ancient nation of Asia, the Medes, which will play an important role in the history of the Middle East, notably in alliance with Persia.
3. The region of Media (the "land of the middle") extends northwest of Persia proper, south and southwest of the Caspian Sea, east of Armenia and Assyria. It is the territory that Madai and his descendants inhabited.
H4074G.origine: The name Madai literally means "land of the middle," due to the geographical location of the region between the Caspian Sea and the great deserts. This character is presented in the genealogy of the peoples that descend from Noah and his three sons: Madai is one of the seven sons of Japheth, one of Noah's three sons.
H4074G.emploi: Madai appears only twice in the Bible, both in genealogical passages: in Genesis 10:2 and in 1 Chronicles 1:5. These two texts identically list the sons of Japheth after the Flood. Madai is the third son named. What interests the Bible is not Madai himself as an individual, but the fact that he is the ancestor of the people of the Medes, a great power of antiquity that will appear in the later history of Israel, notably alongside Persia.
H4074G.portee: The mention of Madai reminds the reader that all the peoples of the earth descend from Noah and his sons, and that God's plan encompasses the history of all human peoples, not just that of Israel. It shows us the universality of the divine purpose over humanity.

sens: Historical region of Western Asia, northwest of Persia
People and empire of the Medes, allies and then conquerors of Persia
Population and kingdom associated with Persian power in biblical texts
H4074H.detail:
1. Media is a geographical region located in Western Asia, northwest of present-day Persia, between the Caspian Sea and the Armenian mountains. It also refers to the land inhabited by the descendants of the Medes, an ancient people who formed a powerful empire. In the book of Esther, it mentions "the commanders of the army of the Persians and the Medes" (Esther 1:3), showing that Media was a major political and military power alongside Persia.
2. The Medes are the people who inhabited this region. They were long-time partners of Persia before being integrated into the Persian empire. The Bible often mentions them alongside the Persians as two inseparable peoples: "the kings of Persia and Media" (Esther 1:14).
3. By extension, "Media" can refer to the empire or kingdom formed by this people, particularly during its alliance with Persia. It is a formidable power in the eyes of the prophets: Isaiah announces "I will make all sighs cease" when mentioning Elam and Media (Isaiah 21:2), suggesting that these empires exert oppressive domination.
H4074H.origine: The name "Media" comes from the people of the Medes, an Indo-European people who settled in the mountainous region of present-day northwestern Iran. The Hebrew word מָדַי (Maday) directly refers to this people and their land. Historically, the Medes formed a rival empire to Persia before being absorbed into the Achaemenid Persian empire, which explains why the Bible regularly mentions them together as two components of the same imperial power.
H4074H.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the book of Esther and in the prophets. In Esther, Media and the Medes represent a powerful people that is part of the empire of which Ahasuerus is king: it speaks of the "princes of Persia and Media" (Esther 1:14) and the "Chronicles of the kings of the Medes and Persians" (Esther 10:2). The prophets mention it as a military and political power: Jeremiah lists "all the kings of Media" among the nations that must drink the cup of divine judgment (Jeremiah 25:25), and Isaiah refers to it as an oppressive force (Isaiah 21:2). Daniel 8:20 identifies the empire of the Medes and Persians in his prophetic vision. Thus, Media appears as a major player in ancient geopolitics, often associated with Persia in the exercise of power.

sens: People descended from Japheth who inhabited the region of Media
Region of Media, territory located northwest of Persia
Empire or political authority of the Medes and Persians
H4074I.detail:
1. The Medes are an ancient people originating from the territory called Media, located northwest of present-day Persia. They are descended from Japheth according to biblical genealogy. When Assyria conquers the kingdom of Israel, it deports the Israelites to the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6), scattering them in this distant territory.
2. Media is the name of this geographical region itself, situated between the Caspian Sea and the great mountain ranges, east of Assyria and northwest of Persia proper. Jeremiah speaks of the "kings of Media" who will march against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:11), showing that it is a distinct political power.
3. By extension, "Medes and Persians" often together designate the dominant political authority, as when Esther 1:19 mentions the "laws of the Persians and the Medes" — a formula that emphasizes the unity and strength of this combined empire.
H4074I.origine: The name "Medes" (מָדַי) literally means "the land of the middle," evoking the geographical position of this region between other territories. The word comes from an ancient root common to the Indo-European peoples who settled in this region around the second millennium B.C. In Hebrew, this name designates both the people and their land, following a common Semitic usage.
H4074I.emploi: The Medes appear 7 times in the Bible, always in important political and military contexts. In 2 Kings 17 and 18, they are mentioned as a destination for the deportation of the northern Israelites defeated by Assyria, a punishment showing the extent of the dispersion imposed by empires. Isaiah 13:17 and Jeremiah 51:11, 28 describe them as the instrument of divine vengeance against Babylon: the Lord stirs up "the kings of Media" to destroy proud Babylon. In the book of Esther, the "laws of the Persians and the Medes" form an inseparable pair symbolizing the unchanging authority of the empire. The context is always that of the deployment of divine power through global empires.
H4074I.portee: For the Christian, the Medes remind us that God controls global empires and uses them to execute His purposes. No human power, no matter how great, can oppose divine plans. The fate of the Israelite deportees in Media also shows the seriousness of divine judgment on sin, while the use of the Medes against Babylon reveals that the Lord directs even pagan kings according to His justice.

sens: Inhabitant of Media, ancient region of Asia northwest of Persia
H4075.detail: 1. A Mede is a man from the people of Media, a historical region located northwest of present-day Persia, between the Caspian Sea and the deserts of the Iranian plateau. It is a powerful people whose empire extends into Asia Minor. In Daniel 11:1, the prophet mentions "Darius the Mede," an important king who reigns after the fall of Babylon and before the Persian empire.
H4075.origine: The name "Mede" comes from Media, a historical region whose name literally means "land of the middle." This people played a major role in the history of the ancient Near East, particularly alongside the Persians in the formation of a vast empire. The Hebrew word מָדָאָה (Mada'ah) simply designates the inhabitant of this region, as one would say "French" for the inhabitants of France.
H4075.emploi: The term "Mede" appears only once in the Bible in Daniel 11:1, where it qualifies the king Darius who reigns after the conquest of Babylon. This is an important historical element: the Medes and Persians formed a joint empire that dominated the Near East in the 6th century B.C. This context helps date Daniel's visions and situates the political events surrounding the return of the Jews from exile.
H4075.portee: For the Christian reader, the mention of the Medes recalls the historical reality of the great powers that governed the world during the captivity of God's people. It shows that even within these pagan empires, God places His prophets and accomplishes His plans. It is an invitation to see that God's hand acts in history, beyond human borders and kingdoms.

sens: ancient people established in the region known as Media, in the west of Asia
inhabitants of this territory, with their laws and customs
empire or political power of the Medes
H4076G.detail: The Medes are an ancient people who occupied a territory located in the northwest of what is now Persia, southwest of the Caspian Sea, between Armenia and Assyria to the west, and the great salt desert to the east. In the book of Daniel, they appear as a major political power: Belshazzar sees in a dream that the kingdom of Babylon will be "divided, and given to the Medes and Persians" (Daniel 5:28). Their historical fame rests mainly on their laws, reputed to be immutable and inviolable: the text repeats three times that "the law of the Medes and Persians" cannot be abrogated (Daniel 6:8, 6:12, 6:15), which underscores their rigid character and absolute authority in the eyes of the ancients.
H4076G.origine: The name "Medes" literally designates the people of the "land of the middle" (Media). It is a real historical people, known to the ancient Greeks and historians: the Medes formed a powerful empire in Western Asia before being gradually absorbed by the Persian empire. The text of Daniel reflects this geopolitical reality of antiquity.
H4076G.emploi: The word "Medes" appears only in the book of Daniel, exactly four times, always in the plural, and always associated with the Persians. Daniel mentions them to describe the end of the Babylonian empire and the advent of a new dominant power. The context is political and legislative: the laws of the Medes and Persians are spoken of as an irrevocable legal institution. The Medes represent here not only a neighboring people but a prestigious and respected legal authority.
H4076G.portee: For the Christian reader, the mention of the Medes and Persians in Daniel is an affirmation of the historical relevance of the book: the prophet speaks of real powers of the known world, not of fantasies. This shows how God controls even the most powerful empires, whose laws seem immutable but remain under His authority. It is an encouragement to trust, even when the forces of the world seem overwhelming.

sens: historical region located northwest of Persia, inhabited by the Medes
H4076H.detail: Media is an ancient region of Western Asia, northwest of what is now Persia. It extends south and southwest of the Caspian Sea, between Armenia and Assyria to the west, and the great salt desert of Iram to the east. Its name means "land of the middle," referring to its geographical position. It is where the Medes lived, a people who played a major role in the ancient history of the Near East. In Ezra 6:2, Media is mentioned as the province where Achmetha, the capital, was located, the city where the decree of Cyrus regarding the reconstruction of the Jerusalem temple was discovered.
H4076H.origine: The Aramaic word מָדַי (Media) comes from the same root as the Hebrew מָדַי from the list of peoples. The name literally means "land of the middle" and refers to the central position of this region between several great ancient powers. The Medes and Persians together formed a powerful empire, and the term "Media" designates the specific territory they inhabited.
H4076H.emploi: Media appears only once in the Bible in Aramaic, in Ezra 6:2, when the decree of King Cyrus is discovered in Achmetha. This passage contextualizes the authorization given to the exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. The mention of this province illustrates the extent of the Persian empire under which the Jews lived at that time, and shows that the official records of the empire were kept in important cities like Achmetha.

sens: Inhabitant of Media, ancient Persian empire
H4077.detail: A Mede was a region of the ancient Near East, located in what is now Iran. A Mede is therefore an inhabitant or citizen of this kingdom. In Daniel 5:31, Darius the Mede seizes the kingdom after the fall of Babylon: he is a king of Median origin or descent who becomes master of Babylonian power.
H4077.origine: The word comes from Aramaic and literally means "land of the middle" or "median land," as Media was situated at the heart of the region between other peoples of the Near East. It is a well-documented historical kingdom, neighboring and rival to Assyria and then Persia.
H4077.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in French, in Daniel 5:31. It designates Darius, presented as a Mede, that is to say belonging to the Median people or dynasty. This usage underscores the political changes of the time: after the fall of Babylon, it is a leader of Median origin who takes control of the kingdom. The Aramaic of the book of Daniel, the diplomatic language of that time, uses this term to precisely identify the origin or ethnicity of the new king.

sens: dispute, conflict between people
habit of disputing, quarrelsome character
drawing lots, decision by chance
H4079.detail:
1. A quarrel is a dispute or conflict between two people or two groups. It arises from a disagreement that escalates in tension: this is why Proverbs 6:14 describes someone who "excites quarrels" by gossiping, and Proverbs 18:19 compares quarrels between brothers to locks that trap a house in conflict.
2. The word also designates the character of someone who constantly quarrels, who loves to dispute. Proverbs 19:13 calls "the quarrels of a woman" this incessant flow of complaints that exhausts like "an endless gutter"; Proverbs 21:9 and 21:19 speak of "sharing the dwelling of a quarrelsome woman," showing that this person makes communal life impossible.
3. Rarely, the word takes on the meaning of "drawing lots" or "decision": in Proverbs 18:18, "the lot causes disputes to cease" by deciding between the powerful, as if chance could calm what reason could not resolve.
H4079.origine: The Hebrew word midyan comes from a root that evokes the idea of separating, dividing, putting in opposition. This is what happens when one disputes: two people divide, separate by anger. The word can also evoke the notion of sharing or distribution, hence its rare use for drawing lots, which "shares" rights among contenders.
H4079.emploi: This word appears about ten times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the book of Proverbs, where it returns as a constant theme of the wise. It primarily designates the quarrel itself, the erupted conflict: someone "excites quarrels" by sowing discord. But it is mostly used to describe the quarrelsome temperament, particularly that of an irritable woman prone to dispute. Proverbs repeatedly addresses this subject, suggesting that a quarrelsome woman makes the home unlivable, to the point that it is better to live alone. The word can also designate the mechanism of drawing lots, intended to peacefully resolve a dispute.
H4079.portee: This word teaches the reader that quarrel is a serious evil that destroys communal life. Proverbs does not merely condemn it: they show that it often arises from the perverse heart of one who loves to "excite" conflicts, and that living with a quarrelsome person is a true torment. For the Christian, it is an invitation to cultivate peace, to avoid sowing discord, and to recognize that certain characters prone to dispute make life unbearable — hence the importance of patient love and soothing words.

sens: Son of Abraham and Keturah
People descended from Midian
Territory inhabited by the Midianites
H4080G.detail:
1. Midian is a son born to Abraham and his concubine Keturah, after the death of Sarah. He is therefore a half-brother of Ishmael and Isaac, and has five brothers: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Jishbak, and Shuach. He himself has five sons: Ephah, Epher, Enoch, Abida, and Eldaa (Genesis 25:2-4).
2. Midian is also the name of the tribe or people that descends from this ancestor, the Midianites, who form a distinct nation in biblical narratives.
3. The territory of Midian refers to the region that this tribe inhabits, primarily a desert in the northern Arabian Peninsula, a distant land where Moses fled after leaving Egypt.
H4080G.origine: The name "Midian" means "strife" or "conflict" in Hebrew, perhaps reflecting tensions or a tumultuous nature. Midian is a son of Abraham through a second union (with Keturah), and his descendants form one of the Arab nations mentioned in the biblical genealogy. His name appears mainly in the genealogical lists of Chronicles and Genesis.
H4080G.emploi: Midian appears four times in the Bible, always in genealogical passages: twice in Genesis 25 and twice in 1 Chronicles 1. These verses enumerate his ancestors (Abraham and Keturah), his brothers, and his own children. He is never the subject of an action, but simply named in the succession of post-Abrahamic generations. This usage reflects the importance of tracing family lines and the peoples that descend from Abraham.

sens: nomadic people of the northern Arabian desert
territory inhabited by this people
inhabitant of Midian
H4080H.detail:
1. Midian is primarily a Bedouin people established in the deserts of the northern Arabian Peninsula, particularly active in trade and raids. Israel knows them mainly through their invasions: in Judges 6, the Midianites devastate the Israelite harvests so forcefully that the text says, "the hand of Midian was heavy against Israel" (Judges 6:2).
2. The name also designates the region controlled by this people, a vast desert territory. Moses found refuge there when he fled Egypt: he marries Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian (Exodus 2:15-16).
3. By extension, a Midianite is an inhabitant of this territory or a member of this nomadic people, like Cozbi, the wife of Zimri mentioned in Numbers 25:15.
H4080H.origine: The name Midian comes from an eponymous ancestor: Midian was a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2). The etymological meaning would be "strife" according to some, reflecting the combative and raiding character of the people. It is the descendants of this Midian who formed the tribe and territory bearing his name.
H4080H.emploi: Midian appears 51 times in the Bible, concentrated mainly in the books of Numbers and Judges. Genesis and Exodus mention it during Moses' exile: he marries there and becomes a shepherd (Exodus 2-3). In Numbers 22-25, the Midianites ally with Balak against Israel and seduce the Israelites into idolatrous worship. The major context is Judges 6-8: for seven years, the Midianites ravage Israel with a considerable army (Judges 6:33: "All Midian, Amalek, and the sons of the East"), until Gideon miraculously defeats them with 300 men (Judges 7-8). These passages portray Midian as a formidable and feared enemy.
H4080H.portee: Midian embodies in the Old Testament the external enemies who oppress the people of God, but also the possibility of deliverance through faith and obedience. The story of Gideon teaches that numbers and human strength do not matter: it is trust in God alone that brings liberation. It also invites spiritual vigilance: as Israel became entangled with the Midianites through idolatry, believers must guard against influences contrary to the faith.

sens: Fortified city of Judah
Locality in the Judean desert
H4081.detail: Middin is a small fortified city of Judah, mentioned as one of the six cities located in the Judean desert. The Bible cites it in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the land distribution (Joshua 15:61).
H4081.origine: The name Middin means "measures" in Hebrew, derived from the root that evokes the idea of delimiting or measuring. This name, like many place names, likely reflects a geographical or administrative characteristic of the locality, perhaps a place of fortification or territorial delimitation.
H4081.emploi: Middin appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:61, where it is listed among the cities of the Judean desert. These six fortified cities in the desert constituted the defensive system of Judah in the arid and border region of the Dead Sea. Middin represents these strategic outposts established in the wild and inhospitable lands.

sens: Region or administrative district under the authority of a chief or governor
Distinct territory of an organized kingdom according to an administrative division
H4082.detail:
1. A province is an administrative region of an empire or kingdom, equipped with its own governors and administrative structures. It is a clearly defined and distinct territory within a larger political entity. The king appoints officials "in all the provinces of his kingdom" to carry out his orders (Esther 2:3), indicating that each province can be reached by a unique royal policy.
2. This term also designates the administrative status of this territory: the organization of a large state into several provinces allows the sovereign to govern effectively by dispersing power to local governors. When it is said that Jerusalem and Judah are recognized after the exile as a "province" (Nehemiah 7:6), their official status within a larger empire is acknowledged. The "provinces of the king" (Esther 9:16) together form the complete domain that the monarch controls.
H4082.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to divide" or "to distribute." A province is indeed a "portion" or "section" of a larger whole — the way in which a territory is divided for easier governance. This Hebrew word has an Aramaic equivalent of the same form, showing its use in the context of the multinational empires of the ancient Near East, notably Persian and Babylonian.
H4082.emploi: This word appears about 40 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical and prophetic books of the post-exilic periods (Nehemiah, Esther, Daniel). It primarily describes the administrative divisions of the Persian and Babylonian empires. In 1 Kings 20, the "governors of the provinces" are military officials of Ahab. The book of Esther uses it extensively (34 occurrences) to show how King Ahasuerus governs his vast territories: his edicts and letters circulate "in every province" so that all his subjects obey (Esther 1:22, 8:13). The planned destruction of the Jews and their eventual salvation pass through this provincial system. In Daniel and Ezekiel, the term also refers to kingdoms or territories under foreign domination.
H4082.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that, even under foreign domination or distant from central power, God's faithful remain under His protection. In Esther particularly, while God's name does not appear, it is His providence that governs the events of all the provinces: the Jews dispersed throughout the empire find, through a reversal of the king, salvation and strength where their destruction was planned. The word also emphasizes the universality of divine control over human empires, which divide the world at their whim but remain under the control of the Most High.

sens: Administrative territory of an empire subject to a central authority
Geographical division of a larger region, with its own government
Region conquered and governed by a foreign power
H4083.detail:
1. A province is an administrative subdivision of a large empire such as the Persian or Babylonian empire. It is placed under the authority of a governor or an official who exercises power on behalf of the king (Daniel 2:48: the king gives Daniel "the command of all the province of Babylon"). It is a well-defined territorial unit, administered in a centralized manner.
2. The term often designates a specific geographical region: the province of Judah, the province of Babylon, the province of Media are precise areas of the ancient world (Ezra 5:8 and 6:2). These provinces may each have a capital or an important administrative center.
3. In the biblical context, provinces are generally lands conquered or placed under foreign domination. Judah itself, although the land of Israel, becomes a province in the Persian administrative system after the Exile (Ezra 5:8: "we went to the province of Judah").
H4083.origine: The Hebrew word מְדִינָה comes from a root that refers to administration and judgment (דִּין, "to judge", "to administer"). It is a term borrowed from the political vocabulary of the empires of Mesopotamia and Persia. The Hebrews adopted it during their contact with these great administrative powers. In Aramaic (the language of the text of Ezra and Daniel that we read), the word has the same form and meaning.
H4083.emploi: The word "province" appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which recount the Exile and the restoration of Judah under foreign domination. These books reflect the administrative organization of the Persian and Babylonian empires. The usages show provinces as political entities governed: Babylon with its wise men (Daniel 2:48-49), Judah after the return from Exile (Ezra 5:8), the various provinces of Media and Babylon under royal control (Ezra 4:15, 6:2, 7:16). The word emphasizes that the people of God live under a foreign political regime, integrated into an imperial administrative structure.
H4083.portee: For the Christian reader, this word recalls a reality of the Exile: the people of God, dispersed and exiled, must live under the domination of other powers. It illustrates humility and trust in God despite the loss of political sovereignty. In the Book of Daniel especially, the "provinces" of Babylon symbolize a world dominated by earthly powers, before which stands the faithfulness of the people of God and the certainty that God maintains sovereign control over history.

sens: Person from the region of Midian
Member of a nomadic tribe of the ancient Near East
Inhabitant of the lands of Midian
H4084.detail:
1. A Midianite is a person from Midian, a region of the ancient Near East located east of Sinai. Reuel and his son Hobab, father-in-law and friend of Moses, are referred to as Midianites (Numbers 10:29).
2. The term also designates the members of the tribe of Midian, presented in the Bible as nomadic peoples with whom Israel had contacts — sometimes peaceful, sometimes conflictual. After a serious infidelity involving Midianite women, God commands Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies and to fight them (Numbers 25:17; 31:2).
H4084.origine: The word comes from Midian (in Hebrew מִדְיָן), whose primary meaning is "strife" or "dispute." Midian is the name of a historical region and its inhabitants. The suffix -י indicates belonging to this region or people, as if to say "one who comes from."
H4084.emploi: The term appears 6 times in the Segond, mainly in Numbers. It is first encountered when Moses lives in Midian (Numbers 10:29), then during the moral crisis described in chapter 25, where a Midianite woman poses a serious problem for Israel (Numbers 25:6, 14, 15). The political context then hardens: God orders Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies (Numbers 25:17; 31:2), showing how relations between Israel and Midian shifted from peaceful coexistence to conflict.
H4084.portee: This name reminds us that ancient Israel was not isolated: it coexisted with other peoples, with whom it could have ties of friendship or alliance, but also serious ruptures. For the believer, this history illustrates the dangers of drifting away from God through impure alliances and the importance of remaining faithful to His commandments, even under social or cultural pressure.

sens: Hollow container used to crush and mix foods or substances
H4085.detail: 1. The mortar is a kitchen utensil, typically made of stone or ceramic, in which food is crushed using a pestle. In Numbers 11:8, the Israelites used the mortar to grind the freshly gathered manna, reducing it to powder before cooking it into cakes. This simple yet essential utensil represents daily domestic work.
H4085.origine: The Hebrew word מְדֹכָה comes from the root דכה (daka), which means "to crush" or "to grind." The mortar derives its name from its function: it is the object in which one crushes. This word reflects an ancient technique of food preparation, well attested throughout the ancient Near East, where the mortar and pestle were essential kitchen tools.
H4085.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew New Testament (Numbers 11:8). In this context, it describes one of the means used by the Israelites to prepare the manna: it could be crushed either with millstones or ground in a mortar. The use of the mortar here shows that even in the desert, the people of Israel had ordinary kitchen utensils to transform food.
H4085.portee: This seemingly mundane detail reminds us that God provides not only for the food of the people but also for their ability to transform and prepare it. The manna was not a magical food ready to eat: it required work and tools. This invites us to see in the ordinary acts of cooking an expression of our trust in God and our responsibility towards our loved ones.

sens: City of Moab threatened with destruction
H4086.detail: Madmen is a city of Moab, a region located east of the Jordan. Its name literally means "manure" or "heap of manure" in Hebrew, evoking a place of waste or refuse. In the prophecy of Jeremiah against Moab, Madmen is mentioned among the cities destined for destruction: the prophet announces that it will be annihilated like the other Moabite cities (Jeremiah 48:2). This mention is part of the divine judgment against the kingdom of Moab for its pride and distance from God.
H4086.origine: The name Madmen comes from the Hebrew root "damam" which means "to be silent" or "to be still," but also from the image of manure or a heap of debris. Despite the obscurity of this name for us, it was probably a real city of Moab, although few other historical sources describe it. The name evokes both humility and perhaps insignificance in the eyes of the one who bears it.
H4086.emploi: Madmen appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 48:2, in a series of prophecies against the cities of Moab. Jeremiah lists the localities that will undergo divine judgment: Heshbon, Madmen, and others. This unique mention shows that Madmen was a real Moabite city, integrated into the urban network of Moab, but which plays no particular role in the biblical narrative outside of this prophetic condemnation.

sens: Heap or place where excrement and waste are accumulated
Dirty and degrading place, symbol of contempt and humiliation
H4087.detail:
1. Manure is primarily a heap or pit where organic waste and excrement from animals or humans accumulate — a reality of rural and agricultural life. In Isaiah 25:10, the prophet describes Moab trampled underfoot "like straw is trampled in a manure pit": the image emphasizes brutal crushing and absolute contempt.
2. Figuratively, manure becomes a symbol of contempt, abjection, and God's judgment. Being thrown into the manure is to be reduced to nothing, publicly humiliated, treated like waste. This cruel image expresses divine anger against those who resist God.
H4087.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of smoking or smelling bad. It literally designates the heap of garbage or the manure pit found near ancient dwellings. The word stands in opposition to everything that is pure, clean, or honorable in biblical culture.
H4087.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 25:10. It is set in the context of a prophecy against Moab, an enemy nation of Israel. God announces that Moab will be crushed and humiliated in a radical way. The image of manure reinforces the contrast between God's greatness and the humiliation of the rebels. It is strong language, which seeks less to describe a concrete act than to express the magnitude of divine judgment.
H4087.portee: For the biblical reader, this image of manure reminds that God overturns the powerful and spares not those who oppose Him. It also invites confession: we are all capable of falling so low. But it primarily calls for a respectful fear of the Lord, whose justice is inevitable.

sens: Benjaminite village north of Jerusalem
H4088.detail: Madmena is a small village located in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. Its name literally means "heap of manure" or "manure," which likely evokes a place of little prestige or an agricultural area. The prophet Isaiah mentions it only once while describing the advance of an enemy army fleeing before God's judgment, listing the villages of Benjamin that it passes through.
H4088.origine: The name Madmena comes from a Hebrew root that evokes garbage, manure, or residue. This type of descriptive name, which designates a place by a characteristic of its soil or environment, was common for villages and hamlets. The word reflects the reality of an agricultural region where manure was used to enrich the fields.
H4088.emploi: Madmena appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 10:31. The prophet lists the villages north of Jerusalem in the order of an army in retreat: "Madmena flees." This passage is part of an oracle announcing God's judgment on the kingdom of Assyria. Although tiny and without its own narrative, this village was a real and known locality to the prophet's audience.

sens: City in the south of Judah
H4089G.detail: Madmanna is a small city located in the southern region of the territory of Judah. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities that Joshua assigns to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:31). Its name means "heap of manure" in Hebrew, which may reflect the lowly or unprestigious character of the place — a geographical name based on a feature of the local landscape.
H4089G.origine: The Hebrew name Madmannah (מַדְמַנָּה) comes from the root daman (דמן), which means "manure" or "dung." The suffix -ah (ה) transforms it into a place name. It is a typical example of a biblical geographical name that simply describes a physical characteristic of the site.
H4089G.emploi: Madmanna appears only once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 15:31, in the enumeration of the cities in southern Judah assigned to the tribe during the division of Canaan. This list places Madmanna among the localities of the Negev, the desert region of southern Judah. The city is also called Beth-Marcaboth ("house of chariots"), suggesting it had a military or administrative function. No particular event is reported about Madmanna in the biblical narrative.

sens: Son of Shaaph, of the lineage of Caleb
City in the south of Judah
H4089H.detail:
1. Madmanna is a man of the tribe of Judah, son of Shaaph. He belongs to the lineage of Caleb and lived during the time of the divided monarchy (1 Chronicles 2:49).
2. Madmanna also designates a locality in the southern district of Judah, mentioned in the genealogy of Caleb as a place of which this man was the father or founder.
H4089H.origine: The name Madmanna means "heap of manure" or "manure," from the Hebrew word "mad" (extended) and "mannah" (manure). It is a concrete and unflattering name that evokes a lowly place, common in the names of ancient Judah cities.
H4089H.emploi: Madmanna appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:49, in the detailed genealogy of Caleb. The context shows that Madmanna was either a son of Shaaph or a place founded or inhabited by this branch of Caleb's family. It is an incidental mention, with no particular narrative associated with this character or place.

sens: Disagreement, dispute between people
Conflict, tension created by hatred or pride
H4090.detail:
1. A quarrel is a disagreement that escalates into a dispute or open conflict between people. This is what the false witness causes when he deliberately sows discord: "the one who stirs up quarrels among brothers" (Proverbs 6:19) delights in breaking harmony through deceitful words.
2. The quarrel also naturally arises from hatred, which inflames conflicts instead of resolving them. In contrast, "love covers all wrongs" (Proverbs 10:12): the one who loves seeks to extinguish quarrels, while the one who hates continually rekindles them.
H4090.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of disputing, contending. It designates the conflict and the trouble it brings into human relationships. It is a word of biblical wisdom, frequently used to describe divisions that should be avoided.
H4090.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Proverbs, which examines the causes and consequences of conflict. It is always presented as something that wisdom denounces: the false witness stirs it up (Proverbs 6:19), and hatred fuels it (Proverbs 10:12). Proverbs thus shows that certain acts or feelings — falsehood, hatred — naturally create quarrels that must be combated with truth and love.
H4090.portee: This word reminds the believer that every deceitful word and every feeling of hatred carries within it the seed of conflict and division. It invites vigilance: not only to avoid seeking quarrel but to recognize what inflames it (falsehood, pride) and to oppose it with truth and love. It is a call to peace within the community, at the very heart of biblical wisdom.

sens: Son of Abraham and Keturah
Brother of Ishmael and Isaac
Ancestor of a people or region
H4091.detail:
1. Medan is one of the sons that Abraham had with Keturah, his second wife after Sarah's death. He appears in Abraham's genealogy as the first in a series of six sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah (Genesis 25:2).
2. He is a half-brother of Ishmael (the son of Abraham and Hagar) and Isaac (the son of Abraham and Sarah). He represents the descendants of Abraham through a different branch than that of the promised covenant.
3. Although little is detailed in the biblical text, Medan is likely the eponymous ancestor of a people or region in the ancient Near East, according to a common practice in biblical genealogies where a person's name becomes that of a nation.
H4091.origine: The name Medan literally means "contention" or "dispute" in Hebrew, which may evoke a situation of conflict or tension. The exact meaning of the name remains tied to its genealogical context: Medan belongs to the descendants of Abraham promised beyond the central covenant, which will pass through Isaac.
H4091.emploi: Medan is mentioned only twice in the Bible: in Genesis 25:2 and in 1 Chronicles 1:32. Both passages provide exactly the same genealogy, listing Medan among the six sons of Abraham and Keturah. Unlike some of his brothers like Midian, who have a more developed posterity in the Old Testament, Medan only appears in these genealogical lists without any mention of his descendants thereafter. He represents a branch of Abraham's lineage that quickly disappears from biblical history.

sens: Member of the tribe of Midian
Inhabitant of the land of Midian
H4092.detail:
1. Midianite: a member of the tribe descended from Midian, son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2). In Genesis 37:36, the Midianites are those who buy Joseph from his brothers and sell him in Egypt to Potiphar.
2. The term also broadly designates any inhabitant of the land of Midian, a region in the southeast Arabian Peninsula, known for its merchants and caravans.
H4092.origine: The word comes from the proper name Midian (מִדְיָן, Midian), son of Abraham and his concubine Keturah. The name Midian likely means "one who judges" or "trial" in Hebrew. His descendants formed a nomadic and trading tribe that became significant in the commercial exchanges of the ancient Near East.
H4092.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Genesis 37:36, in the account of Joseph sold by his brothers. The Midianites, passing merchants, buy Joseph and resell him in Egypt. This people is mentioned several times in the Old Testament as a neighboring people of Israel, often in commercial relations or in conflict.

sens: Knowledge, acquired understanding, body of knowledge
Ability of the mind to understand and judge
Thought, inner reflection, movement of the soul
H4093.detail:
1. Intelligence is primarily knowledge, an understanding: it is what one has learned or comprehended. In Chaldea, God gives the four young men a "science," meaning the ability to master all letters and wisdom (Daniel 1:17).
2. It is also the mental faculty itself: the ability to think, understand, and judge. Solomon asks God for "wisdom and intelligence" to govern the people and "know how to conduct himself" (2 Chronicles 1:10) — it is not just about possessing information, but having a clear mind to act sensibly.
3. Finally, it is thought itself, the secret movement of the soul. Ecclesiastes speaks of a curse that one might form "in his thought" (Ecclesiastes 10:20) — this intimate thought that the heart ruminates in silence.
H4093.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to know" or "to understand," and designates the very seat of knowledge in the human soul. It is close to other biblical words for wisdom and intelligence, but emphasizes the process of understanding rather than moral virtue. This term belongs to the vocabulary of discernment and reflection.
H4093.emploi: This word appears six times in biblical Hebrew, mostly in late wisdom and historical texts. In Solomon (2 Chronicles 1:10-12), it denotes the divine gift of understanding and judgment, closely related to wisdom, for just governance. Daniel and his companions receive "science" — a form of intelligence capable of mastering high knowledge (Daniel 1:17). In Ecclesiastes 10:20, the word is lowered to the sense of simple inner thought, that which is kept hidden. The usage thus progresses from scholarly knowledge to the simple movement of reflection.
H4093.portee: This word reminds the reader that all true intelligence comes from God and is not merely the accumulation of knowledge: it is a capacity of the heart to understand, judge, and act with discernment. Asking for intelligence, like Solomon, is to recognize that technical knowledge without wisdom is insufficient. It also invites vigilance over one's secret thoughts, knowing that God knows the heart.

sens: blow or stab that pierces
word that wounds like a sharp weapon
H4094.detail:
1. The word literally designates a violent blow that pierces, a sting or wound caused by a sharp weapon. It is the action of striking with a sharp object that penetrates the flesh.

2. In Proverbs 12:18, this word moves from the physical domain to the realm of words: "There is one who speaks rashly, like the thrusts of a sword." Reckless words, thrown without thought, are compared to blows from a blade that pierce and wound the soul and heart of the one who hears them. In contrast, the "tongue of the wise" soothes and heals.
H4094.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to pierce, to thrust, to sting." It evokes the image of a pointed object that crosses or penetrates a surface. This root belongs to the semantic field of violence and penetration, and the word madqarah specifically designates the result or act of this penetration.
H4094.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 12:18. In this wisdom verse, it serves to illustrate the destructive power of reckless speech. Hebrew sages use concrete and violent imagery to teach the moral value of controlling the tongue. This comparison between physical injury and moral injury underscores that words can cause harm as real and lasting as that of a weapon.
H4094.portee: This verse reminds the Christian that their words are never neutral: they can wound deeply or heal. The lightness of speech, the absence of reflection before speaking, turns every word into a weapon of destruction. Conversely, one who masters their tongue and speaks wisely soothes and restores. It is an invitation to exercise constant vigilance over our speech and a call to measure the real impact of our words on those who listen to us.

sens: Vertical or very steep face of a mountain or rock
High and difficult-to-access place, natural refuge
Imposing rocky obstacle
H4095.detail:
1. A sheer cliff is a very steep, almost vertical rock face that rises abruptly. In Song of Solomon 2:14, the beloved dove hides "in the clefts of the rock" and "in the sheer cliffs," images of a safe and secret refuge hidden in the heart of the mountain.
2. It is also a naturally fortified place, difficult to access for someone who does not know the way — an ideal hiding spot to escape danger. The rock face offers protection and isolation.
3. In Ezekiel 38:20, during the divine judgment on Gog, "the cliffs of the rocks will fall," showing that even the most imposing rocky obstacles cannot withstand the power of God.
H4095.origine: The Hebrew word מַדְרֵגָה (madregah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of ascending or climbing — like a step or a degradation of terrain. This notion is found in the word "degrees," these steps that allow one to climb a slope. It is thus a rock formation whose steep and sheer character makes it an obstacle or a refuge.
H4095.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Song of Solomon 2:14, it refers to the rocky refuge where the beloved hides, a poetic and symbolic refuge of safety. In Ezekiel 38:20, it appears in an apocalyptic vision of judgment, where the rocky cliffs collapse under the manifestation of divine power. In both cases, it is an impressive geological formation, but its role changes: sometimes a refuge, sometimes a temporary obstacle before God.
H4095.portee: This sheer cliff reminds us that God recognizes and protects those who hide in Him, even in the most remote and inaccessible places. It also shows that nothing — not even the most solid natural obstacles — can withstand the sovereign power of God when He intervenes to judge.

sens: place where one walks, where one puts their foot
territory where one circulates
domain that one traverses
H4096.detail:
1. The word first designates a physical place where one can walk and put their foot without obstacle. It is a passage, a walkable path.

2. By extension, it refers to a territory where one circulates freely, which one regularly traverses — in Deuteronomy 2:5, God tells Israel that He will not give them even "the width of a footstep" of the territory of Edom, showing that a "passageway" is primarily a space whose access and circulation are controlled.

3. The term can also refer to a domain or place that belongs to us, which can be trodden and crossed at will — here the idea is that Israel cannot set foot in Edom because it is not their land.
H4096.origine: The word comes from the root דרך (darak), "to walk, to tread," from which comes "one who walks" and also "path, way." Midrakh is a nominalized action term: literally "the act of walking." The same root is found in "Derech" (path, way), which is very common in the Bible.
H4096.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 2:5. Moses reminds Israel of the divine words: God denies Israel even the smallest portion of the territory of Edom, "the width of a shoe's sole" — no passageway belongs to them there. It is a concrete and restrictive term that emphasizes that Israel must respect the borders of Edom and not encroach upon its lands.
H4096.portee: For the reader, this term reminds us that the borders between peoples are set by God and must be respected. Israel, as powerful as it may be, cannot appropriate the territories of others: not even the right to walk there. It is a lesson in humility and submission to divine order.

sens: Written account, chronicle, history recorded in writing
Didactic or explanatory work, midrash
H4097.detail:
1. The word designates a written account or chronicle: it is a historical or narrative report. In 2 Chronicles 13:22, the text mentions the "memoirs" of the prophet Iddo, that is, the writings where the acts and words of King Abijah are recorded — historical documents that serve as a source for understanding what happened.

2. The word can also refer to a didactic or explanatory work, a thoughtful exposition (what is called midrash in Hebrew): a text intended to instruct and explain. In 2 Chronicles 24:27, the "memoirs" recount not only the events of the reign of Amaziah but also "the great number of prophecies he received," which shows that it is a reflection on the meaning of history, not just a simple list of facts.
H4097.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root דרש (darash), which means "to seek," "to study," "to search for meaning." The prefix מִ (mi) indicates action or result. Thus, מִדְרָשׁ (midrash) literally means "the search" or "the study," hence "exposition" or "didactic writing." It is a term that designates an interpretive and understanding approach to the text, and by extension, a work resulting from this search.
H4097.emploi: The word appears twice in Chronicles, always in the plural ("memoirs"). It designates written sources that the author of Chronicles uses to recount the history of the kings of Judah. These sources come from prophets (like Iddo) or collectives ("the book of the kings"). The context shows that these are authorized and reliable documents, worthy of serving as a basis for the biblical narrative. The word also reveals the author's conviction that history is not neutral: it contains a teaching about the will of God (notably through prophecies).
H4097.portee: This word reminds us that in the Old Testament, history and teaching are inseparable: the Bible recounts what happened, but always to help us understand the hand of God at work. The "memoirs" of the prophet Iddo are not dead archives, but texts aimed at enlightening our faith. This invites us to read biblical history seeking what it tells us about God and His will, as the authors of Chronicles themselves did.

sens: what has been separated from the husk by threshing
the people of Israel treated like grain on the threshing floor
what has undergone brutal and purifying treatment
H4098.detail:
1. The word literally designates the grain after it has been threshed on the floor — that moment when the grain, separated from the chaff, lies on the ground before winnowing. It is the product of threshing, what remains when the ears are struck.

2. Isaiah uses it to speak of the people of Israel: "my people, who have been threshed like grain in my threshing floor." Israel, mistreated by trials and invasions, is compared to grain on which the flail has been raised. It is an image of suffering and humiliation.

3. But this suffering is not in vain: threshing separates the good grain from the useless chaff. In this biblical image, there is the idea of sorting, of a painful but necessary purification. The threshed people can thus be purified and renewed.
H4098.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to beat" or "to strike." It is a feminine passive participle: the form of the word emphasizes that the grain has undergone the action of threshing. The image of threshing was very familiar to the Israelites: it was the normal way to separate the grains of wheat or barley from their husks.
H4098.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 21:10. The prophet Isaiah reports what the Lord revealed to him about the sufferings of Israel. He uses this term precisely to express how the people have been treated like threshed grain — a strong and concrete image that spoke to the peasants and farmers who listened to the prophet. It is a poetic and symbolic formula to describe national affliction.
H4098.portee: This image of threshed grain on the floor reminds believers that trials — even brutal ones — are never without purpose. God does not allow His people to suffer randomly: threshing purifies and prepares the harvest. For the Christian today, it is a word of comfort when going through difficult times: difficulties can be the means of purifying and drawing closer to God.

sens: Father of Haman
High-ranking figure at the court of King Ahasuerus
H4099.detail:
1. Hammedatha is the father of Haman, the minister whom King Ahasuerus elevated in rank and placed above all the officials (Esther 3:1). His name appears only as a patronymic, always mentioned to identify his feared son.
2. Hammedatha himself remains a shadowy figure: nothing is known of him except that he fathered Haman, the Agagite, the man who became the enemy of the Jews and devised a plan to destroy them (Esther 9:24). His name is cited only in connection with the crimes of his son.
H4099.origine: The name means "double" in Hebrew. Hammedatha is a historical figure from the time of the exile and the return of the Jews, mentioned only in the book of Esther. His precise identity and his specific role in the history of Persia remain unknown; he exists in the biblical text only as the father of Haman.
H4099.emploi: Hammedatha appears only 5 times in the Bible, all in the book of Esther, and invariably as the father of Haman. In each mention, the expression "son of Hammedatha" serves to fully identify Haman and to emphasize his heritage. The texts also refer to him as an "Agagite," a lineage that points to the hereditary enemies of Israel. Hammedatha himself never speaks, never acts: he exists only as a genealogical link connecting Haman to a hostile past.

sens: Sudden and intense fear that seizes someone
Feeling of terror that spreads and dominates a group or region
State of widespread panic at the moment of a threat
Atmosphere of fear and disarray
H4032.detail:
1. Sudden and intense fear that seizes someone: the word designates this violent fright that grips a person in the face of danger or the enemy. It is a visceral reaction, a seizing of the body and mind.
2. Feeling of terror that spreads and dominates a group or region: the terrified is not isolated; it spreads among populations, establishing itself as a threatening presence. In Jeremiah 6:25, the divine order is not to go out "for there is the sword of the enemy, and terror reigns all around," showing how fear occupies an entire territory.
3. State of widespread panic at the moment of a threat of invasion or catastrophe: during enemy attacks, when the sword approaches, terror seizes even the brave. In Jeremiah 46:5, even the strong warriors flee "without looking back... terror is on all sides."
4. Atmosphere of social fear and distrust: terror can also arise from plots, slander, and betrayals. In Psalms 31:14 and Jeremiah 20:10, the one targeted by intrigues finds themselves surrounded by this collective fear that fuels rumors and accusations.
H4032.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing a brutal shock, a jolt. It describes this physical and emotional sensation of violent fear that shakes the whole being. The Hebrew biblical context gives great importance to this terror in the face of concrete threats: invasion, famine, sword, persecution. It is a tangible fear, not an abstract worry.
H4032.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, especially in Jeremiah (5 occurrences), where it describes the atmosphere of terror in the last days before the Babylonian exile. In Psalms 31:14, it refers to the fear that arises from plots. In Jeremiah 20:4, God announces that He will deliver the prophet to "terror" itself, as to an enemy power that engulfs everything. In Jeremiah 6:25 and 46:5, it characterizes moments of military debacle where even the most seasoned warriors are overwhelmed. The word always emphasizes a massive, collective fear that paralyzes or disperses.
H4032.portee: Understanding this word means grasping that fear, in the Bible, is not a shameful weakness but an inevitable reality in the face of evil, injustice, and threat. It becomes a source of wisdom when it leads one to turn to God rather than to weapons or human cunning. For the believer reading these texts of exile or persecution, terror is never the final word: God remains Lord, even when fear reigns around.

sens: Place where one dwells as a foreigner, without being a property owner
Fact of living in a country as a foreigner, temporary passage
Entire life understood as a pilgrimage, a crossing of the world
H4033.detail:
1. The word first designates a physical place: the country where one resides without possessing it, just as a temporary inhabitant. Abraham and Jacob receive the promise of the land of Canaan, but the text describes them as "dwelling as foreigners" there — they reside, indeed, but always as travelers temporarily settled (Genesis 17:8). This is different from a definitive possession: it is a presence, but fragile and temporary.
2. The word then characterizes the entire state of the one who sojourns: the experience of living somewhere without having deep roots. When Esau and Jacob can no longer coexist, the text says that "the land where they sojourned could not support them" (Genesis 36:7) — it is the very act of living there, the lifestyle of the resident without attachment.
3. Jacob, at the end of his life, speaks of his "days of pilgrimage" to designate his entire life: one hundred thirty years of existence lived as a journey, a passage (Genesis 47:9). The word becomes an image of human destiny — we traverse the world without staying, we are all strangers here below.
H4033.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to reside as a foreigner, to sojourn." It is related to the name "ger," the foreigner who temporarily dwells in a country that is not theirs. The word designates less a simple passage than an installation with an awareness of its provisional nature: one lives there, but knows that one will not be there forever. It is the condition of those who live in a country without being full citizens.
H4033.emploi: The word appears ten times, mainly at the beginnings of the Bible. It is used to describe the condition of Abraham and his descendants in Canaan: they live there (sometimes for decades), but as foreigners under divine protection, not as masters of the land. Jacob qualifies his entire life as a "pilgrimage," which shows that the word also denotes a duration, a period. In Genesis 47:9, Jacob uses it twice to encompass the one hundred thirty years of his life: the word extends from space (the place) to time (a whole existence lived in transit). It is the experience of the believer who recognizes themselves as a stranger in this world.
H4033.portee: This word helps the believer understand their position on earth: like Abraham and Jacob, they are temporary residents, pilgrims. Life is not a definitive installation, but a passage toward a promised destination. This perspective invites trust and detachment from material possessions: if we are strangers here, our true riches and our true home are elsewhere, with God.

sens: Sudden and intense fear, sharp dread
That which provokes fear, object of dread
Anxious concern, worry
H4034.detail:
1. Fear is a sudden and sharp fear that seizes someone — an intense dread of the heart. In Psalms 34:5, the psalmist speaks of being delivered from all his fears, meaning all the terrors that oppressed him.
2. The word also designates what one fears, the object that provokes fear within us. In Proverbs 10:24, what the wicked dread (their fear, what they apprehend) is precisely what happens to them — their fear becomes reality.
3. Fear can express a persistent worry, an anxious concern of the soul in the face of what might happen.
H4034.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of trembling and inner turmoil. It is a name formed to describe the emotional state of one who is afraid. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms expressing fear and dread, alongside words like yirah (fear) and pachad (terror).
H4034.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Old Testament. In Psalms 34:5, it expresses the multiple fears from which the believer is liberated by the intervention of the Lord. In Proverbs 10:24, it designates the secret worry of the wicked — what they dread — contrasted with the satisfied desires of the righteous. In both cases, fear is presented as something inevitable for one who does not seek refuge in God, or whose heart is separated from justice.
H4034.portee: This word reminds us that fear and anxiety are human realities that God sees and acknowledges. For the believer, it shows that seeking the Lord leads to deliverance from the fears that gnaw at the heart — not to the absence of difficulties, but to regained peace. For the wicked, it emphasizes that the absence of inner justice generates a dull worry, an inevitable fear.
